degradative autophagic vacuoles (Avd), in human HEK293 cells
treated with CD0345-E003, CD0354-A010 and WNN0090-F002
using transmission electron microscopy (Supplementary Fig. 4).
As a negative control, we selected compounds with high-
conﬁdence bioprocess target predictions that did not overlap with
autophagy-related pathways, excluding compounds with struc-
tures that resemble those predicted to modulate autophagy. None
of 26 control compounds induced GFP-LC3 puncta formation
(Fig. 4f and Supplementary Fig. 5). Furthermore, the mean PCC
value for the chemical-genetic proﬁles of the 14 compounds with
autophagic activity was 0.568, which was higher than that of
complete set of 38 predicted compounds (0.456), suggesting that
chemical-genetic proﬁle similarity has a positive impact on
experimental validation: for the autophagy bioprocess, a com-
pound with a higher correlation score is more likely to be
validated biologically.
Mapping the validated compounds linked to autophagy onto
the CNCL chemical-genetic interaction network, we observed
compounds with distinct validation phenotypes segregating into
two groups. Two compounds (WNN0090-F002 and CD0345-E003)
that had positive LC3 ﬂuorescence microscopy, Western blot and
transmission electron microscopy results mapped to the DNA
replication/repair and mitosis/chromosome segregation biopro-
cesses in the network (Fig. 2b). Recently, it has been shown that
agents causing different types of DNA damage can lead to
targeted autophagy by activating the yeast Mec1/ATR, Tel1/ATM,
and Rad53/CHEK2 kinase cascade [35]. However, the majority of
the
compounds
(CD0295-C003,
CD0296-D002,
CD0296-H004,
CD0296-H007, CD0338-F007, CD0447-G005, WNN0040-A007, and
WNN0159-G002), validated by ﬂuorescence
microscopy
and
Western blotting, were linked to genes in the vesicular trafﬁc
bioprocess (Fig. 2b), which plays a major role in numerous aspects
of autophagy [36]. The bioprocess predictions for these com-
pounds included “ATP hydrolysis coupled proton transport” and
“vacuolar acidiﬁcation”, relating to the lysosomal H+ ATPase,
whose activity is required for proper autophagic ﬂux [36]. Taken
together, these data show that our yeast chemical-genetic
proﬁling platform provides a powerful approach for predicting
compounds that modulate autophagy in human cells.
Wnt/β-catenin
pathway.
We
also
examined
the
effect
of
compounds that had proﬁle similarities with FH535, a known
inhibitor of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, in human cells [23].
FH535 suppresses β-catenin/TCF-mediated transcription and
exhibits anti-proliferative effects in various cancer cell lines.
Although this pathway is not present in yeast [37], we found
that chemical-genetic proﬁles associated with 18 CNCL com-
pounds were signiﬁcantly correlated with the chemical-genetic
proﬁle of FH535 (Fig. 3). Wnt/β-catenin signaling is an important
pathway that inﬂuences cell differentiation, proliferation and
fate [37, 38]. β-catenin activity in this pathway can be grouped
into two processes: accumulation and nuclear transposition. The
former is linked with phosphorylation, while the latter results in
the
formation
of
the
β-catenin-TCF/LEF1
complex,
which
activates transcription of downstream genes. Based on this, we
conducted a reporter gene assay to investigate the effects of
predicted compounds on β-catenin downstream transcription
controlled by β-catenin-TCF/LEF1 complex [39], and Western
blot analysis to determine compound effects on β-catenin
accumulation
and
phosphorylation
mediated
by
glycogen
synthase kinase (GSK) [40].
For the ﬁrst assay, we used cells with the TCF/LEF1 promoter
element linked to the luciferase reporter gene, and measured
luciferase activity after compound treatment. Like FH535, which
decreased luciferase activity by 72.08% after 24-h treatment at
20 μM, luminescence intensity was reduced by CD0450-A007
(39.61%),
3215-1
A11 (61.64%),
and
3305-2
G4
(53.08%),
respectively
(Fig.
5a),
suggesting
that
these
compounds
inhibited transcription from Wnt/β-catenin signaling responsive
elements (TCF/LEF1). We also studied the effects of these
compounds on the expression level of β-catenin. While there
was no signiﬁcant difference between CD0450-A007 and 3215-1
A11 and the DMSO control, 3305-2 G4 treatment clearly
decreased β-catenin expression, consistent with reduced luci-
ferase activity in the TCF/LEF1 reporter assay (Fig. 5b). Dose-
response experiments for luciferase activity demonstrated that
3305-2 G4 and FH535 had a similar IC50 (7.44 μM vs. 7.43 μM,
Fig. 5c), a ﬁnding that was further supported by Western blot
analysis (Fig. 5d). Thus, both FH535 and 3305-2 G4 altered the
expression of active β-catenin. For negative controls, the effects
of 24 random compounds were examined similarly, and while
two compounds displayed FH535-like inhibition in the luciferase
assay,
namely
CD0203-G006
(68.69%)
and
CD0251-G005
(71.75%, Fig. 5e), none of the random compounds exhibited
any impact on β-catenin expression (Fig. 5f).
3305-2 G4 is a known alkaloid called drupacine [41] (Fig. 5c),
isolated
from
Cephalotaxus
fortunei,
whose
structure
was
identiﬁed by spectroscopic data analysis [42]. 3305-2 G4
mapped to “mRNA processing” (Fig. 2b), while FH535 mapped
to “glycosylation, protein folding and targeting, cell wall
biogenesis” bioprocesses (Fig. 2b). However, a closer examina-
tion of high-conﬁdence target process predictions for these
compounds showed that FH535 and 3305-2 G4 share a common
process prediction, “Response to acidic pH” (Supplementary
Table 5). The top driver genes for this target prediction are BCK1
and SLT2, which encode MAPKKK and MAPK of the protein
kinase C signaling pathway in yeast that controls cell wall
integrity [43]. Though the Wnt pathway, the human target for
FH535, is not present in yeast, it is possible that FH535 and 3305-
2 G4 both act on a conserved pathway that is relevant to Wnt
signaling mechanism.
To further assess the shared targets of FH535 and 3305-2 G4, a
“pseudo-compound” chemical-genetic proﬁle was calculated as
a weighted mean proﬁle of the two compounds, which
accentuates large chemical-genetic interaction scores that are
common between FH535 and 3305-2 G4. The mean chemical-
genetic proﬁle of FH535 and 3305-2 G4 was weighted by an
element-wise product between the two compounds. Direct
targets were predicted for this pseudo-compound proﬁle, using
the same process applied to calculate direct targets for real
compounds. Among the top gene targets calculated for the
merged FH535/3305-2 G4 chemical-genetic proﬁle were CDC73
(top 5th out of 4625 ranked genes, Supplementary Table 6) and
MRK1 [18] (top 6th out of 4625 ranked genes, Supplementary
Table 6). CDC73 is a component of the PAF1 complex which
binds to and modulates the activity of RNA polymerases I and II,
and is required for gene expression, histone modiﬁcation, and
telomere maintenance [44]. Its human homolog, paraﬁbromin, is
a tumor suppressor linked to parathyroid, renal, and uterine
cancers [45]. Paraﬁbromin and other components of the PAF1
complex are required for the nuclear transduction of the Wnt
signal, and bind directly to the C-terminal portion of β-catenin
to control the activity of Wnt target genes [46]. MRK1 is one of
four GSK-3 homologs in yeast, and activates Msn2-dependent
transcription of stress responsive genes that function in protein
degradataion [47]. GSK-3 is a key enzyme in Wnt signaling, and
phosphorylates β-catenin leading to its subsequent degradation
[48]. In spite of the Wnt pathway itself being absent in yeast, the
merged chemical-genetic proﬁles of FH535 and 3305-2 G4 were
capable of predicting direct gene targets which are highly
conserved and are important players in Wnt signal transduction.
DISCUSSION
Mode-of-action
discovery
for
novel
compounds
is
a
well-
recognized rate-limiting factor for rational drug development.

Chemical-genetic proﬁling in yeast identiﬁes target pathways in
an unbiased manner and has proven to be amenable to HTS
campaigns,
though
the
utility
of
this
method
in
ﬁnding
compounds that impinge on metazoan pathways, especially those
that are absent from yeast but found in higher organisms, remains
relatively unexplored. The present analysis annotates a complex
library of small molecules employing a diagnostic chemical
genomic pipeline [18]. We used a comprehensive database of
yeast genetics interactions [14] as a key for interpreting the
chemical-genetic proﬁles and linking the predicted compounds to
general
target
bioprocesses.
Indeed,
when
16
compounds
predicted to target the tubulin cytoskeleton assembly pathway
were evaluated using techniques such as cell cycle analysis, two of
them were successfully validated to disrupt tubulin function in
HeLa cells (Supplementary Fig. 2). Importantly, we also developed
a dataset of chemical-genetic proﬁles for approved drugs with
known modes of action, and applied it to identify new hits whose
chemical-genetic proﬁles are highly similar to those of known
drugs with well-established pharmacology in metazoans. Notably,
we have shown that matching the chemical-genetic proﬁles of hits
from HTS campaigns to those of known drugs allows the
identiﬁcation of compounds with targeted activity in mammalian
cell pathways.
As proof of concept, several drugs with highly conserved
cellular targets have chemical-genetic target gene and process
predictions that are consistent with their known modes of action.
Idarubicin, delanzomib, and mocetinostat act on diverse cellular
targets (topoisomerase II, proteasome, and histone deacetylase,
respectively), and these compounds were accurately linked to
their target pathways and bioprocesses in yeast, namely, DNA
replication and repair, proteasome/protein degradation, and
mRNA processing (Fig. 2b).
Correlation analysis of chemical-genetic proﬁles, which com-
pared approved drugs and CNCL compounds, was effective in
linking novel compounds to autophagy, a highly conserved
pathway from yeast to human, and the Wnt/β-catenin signaling

pathway, which is not present in yeast. The autophagy-linked
compounds generally had higher PCC values (~0.8) than that of
the Wnt-linked compounds (~0.35). The difference in distribution
of these values likely reﬂects the high degree of conservation
between autophagy mediators in yeast and metazoans. Thus, this
guilt-by-association analysis may be particularly powerful for
ﬁnding compounds that work in essential, highly conserved
biological pathways.
One distinct advantage of this approach is the ability to group
compounds into functional categories that may reﬂect their
mode-of-action in cells. A striking observation was the segregation
of the autophagy-linked compounds into two regions of the
chemical-genetic
interaction
network:
the
“vesicular
trafﬁc”
bioprocess for a majority of the compounds that were only
validated
by puncta
formation
as
viewed
by
ﬂuorescence
microscopy and a general measurement of LC3-II expression by
Western blotting, and the “DNA replication and repair” and
“nuclear-cytoplasmic transport” parts of the network for com-
pounds that had positive validation results for the more rigorous
assays
to
assess
autophagic
activity
(transmission
electron
microscopy and a LC3-II expression time course). The functional
segregation of these validated hits may reﬂect commonalities in
mode-of-action that would not have been apparent from an assay
that focuses on a single phenotypic outcome such as autophagic
vesicle formation.
Interestingly, the autophagy-modulating compounds can all be
described as cationic amphiphilic drugs (CADs) with common
physiochemical
properties.
CADs
have
a
hydrophobic
ring
structure and a hydrophilic side chain with a charged cationic
amine group, and comprise a diverse array of various substance
classes such as antiarrhythmics and antipsychotics [49]. It has
been recently shown that high concentrations of CADs after long
exposure times tend to localize at autophagosomal compartments
[50]. Accumulation of the tested CADs into the autophagosome
may, at least in part, explain the observed modulation of
autophagy by these compounds.
We also identiﬁed compounds that act on the Wnt/β-catenin
signaling pathway, which is completely absent in yeast, pointing
to the possibility of using yeast chemical-genetic proﬁle similarity
as a way to link compounds to drugs that may not have conserved
yeast targets. Notably, FH535 and 3305-2 G4 map to separate
parts of the chemical-genetic interaction network: “Glycosylation,
protein folding, and cell wall biogenesis” for the former and
“mRNA processing” for the latter (Fig. 2). This suggests that these
compounds have distinct functional consequences in yeast,
though there is signiﬁcant overlap in their chemical-genetic
proﬁles, leading to a PCC value of ~0.35 (P = 1.05 × 10−8).
Interestingly, by merging the chemical-genetic proﬁles of FH535
and 3305-2 G4 and weighting the interaction scores to emphasize
the overlap between their proﬁles, we predicted direct target
yeast genes (CDC73 and MRK1) whose human homologs are key
players in Wnt signaling pathway which either bind to β-catenin
directly to activate expression of target genes upon transduction
of the signal into the nucleus (paraﬁbromin, homolog of CDC73),
or stimulate cytoplasmic degradation of β-catenin by phosphor-
ylation (GSK-3, homolog of MRK1). Furthermore, 3305-2 G4 is a
known natural compound (drupacine) that is capable of suppres-
sing cancer cell growth in vitro [51]. Whether this effect is related
to Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway remains to be explored.
Orthologous phenotypes have been previously used for systema-
tic discovery of non-obvious human disease models [52], and our
study provides a framework for identifying orthologous chemical-
genetic gene targets in yeast for compounds that act on
therapeutically relevant non-conserved pathways in humans.
In conclusion, our ﬁndings demonstrate that compounds with
target bioprocess predictions identiﬁed in an unbiased yeast-
based chemical-genetic system can be validated in mammalian
cells. These target predictions can be derived directly for highly
conserved cell functions, or they can be inferred from chemical-
genetic proﬁles of therapeutics with known modes of action. This
general
approach
shows
great
promise
for
utilizing
yeast
chemical-genetic proﬁling for identifying pathway-speciﬁc drug
leads towards a wide variety of human diseases.

SYSTEMS BIOLOGY
Dual transposon sequencing profiles the genetic  
interaction landscape in bacteria
Justin J. Zik, Morgan N. Price, Keisha Hanifa Alma Mayra, Audrey A. Santoso, Adam P. Arkin,  
Adam M. Deutschbauer, Lok-­To Sham* 
INTRODUCTION: Next-­generation DNA sequencing (NGS) has 
considerably increased the amount of sequencing data in public 
databases. However, millions of these sequences still remain as 
genetic “dark matter.” About one-­third of bacterial genes have no 
known functions, partly due to challenges such as gene redundancy. 
We report dual transposon sequencing (dual Tn-­seq), a high-­
throughput platform designed to systematically mine genetic 
interactions and help identify gene functions. Understanding these 
unknown genes is especially important for developing new 
strategies to combat the growing threat of antimicrobial resistance.
RATIONALE: Transposon sequencing (Tn-­seq) is a widely used, 
unbiased approach for studying gene function. This technique 
measures changes in the abundance of randomly inserted, gene-­
inactivating transposons within a saturated mutant pool, helping to 
identify genes necessary for survival under different conditions. One 
approach is to perform Tn-­seq in a single-­gene knockout background 
to uncover genetic interactions, in which combinations of mutations 
lead to unexpected results such as synthetic lethality. Genes that 
interact are often functionally related. However, traditional Tn-­seq is 
not designed to systematically identify genetic interaction networks 
because it cannot detect random double transposon mutants that are 
far apart in the genome, which limits its scope.
RESULTS: To address this limitation, we developed dual Tn-­seq, 
which enables high-­throughput fitness assessment of a large pool of 
double transposon mutants. Dual Tn-­seq combines randomly 
barcoded (RB) Tn-­seq with the cre-­lox system. Cre recombinase 
brings the two distant barcodes close together, allowing for the 
capture of both insertions within a single sequencing read. We applied 
this system to the human pathogen Streptococcus pneumoniae by 
building two barcoded transposon libraries and combining them to 
generate more than a billion double mutants. After inducing Cre 
and sequencing, we used a probabilistic model to compare observed 
double mutant frequencies with the expected levels calculated  
from the frequencies of the individual mutants. This screen reported 
244 high-­confidence genetic interactions, ranging from synthetic 
lethality to partial growth impairment. These interactions involved 
diverse biochemical pathways, allowing us to define functions of 
hypothetical genes, such as the alternative CTP synthase PyrJ and a 
regulator of peptidoglycan synthesis.
CONCLUSION: Dual Tn-­seq provides a scalable and cost-­effective 
approach to uncover genetic interactions in bacteria. It only 
requires a few components: an inducible promoter, the ability to 
generate transposon mutants, and a functioning cre cassette. As 
sequencing costs continue to decline, this approach will become 
more accessible in a wide range of organisms. Moreover, the scope 
of dual Tn-­seq can be broadened by growing the double mutant 
libraries under different conditions, such as with antibiotic 
treatments or various nutritional and growth conditions. Dual 
Tn-­seq opens new avenues for exploring microbiology and accelerating 
the discovery of drug targets. 

SYSTEMS BIOLOGY
Dual transposon sequencing 
profiles the genetic interaction 
landscape in bacteria
Justin J. Zik1, Morgan N. Price2, Keisha Hanifa Alma Mayra1,  
Audrey A. Santoso1, Adam P. Arkin2,3, Adam M. Deutschbauer2,4, 
Lok-­To Sham1* 
Gene redundancy complicates systematic characterization  
of gene function as single-­gene deletions may not produce 
discernible phenotypes. We report dual transposon sequencing 
(dual Tn-­seq), a platform for assaying the fitness of a 
comprehensive double mutant pool in parallel. Dual Tn-­seq 
couples random barcode transposon site sequencing with the 
Cre-­lox system, enabling deep sampling of 73% of the 1.3 million 
possible double gene deletions in Streptococcus pneumoniae. 
The genetic interactions identified span a wide range of 
biochemical processes, revealing new factors in presumably 
well-­studied pathways, exemplified by a cytidine triphosphate 
synthase PyrJ. Moreover, this approach should permit further 
investigation of growth condition–specific genetic interactions. 
Because dual Tn-­seq does not require the construction of a 
large array of single mutants, it should be readily adaptable to 
various microorganisms.
Knowing the sequence of a gene does not necessarily imply under-
standing its function. Even in the best-­studied bacterium, Escherichia 
coli, about one-­third of its genes encode “proteins of unknown func-
tion” and “hypothetical proteins.” (1) Traditional approaches for elu-
cidating gene function, such as phenotyping deletion mutants, are 
relatively time-­consuming and labor-­intensive. Furthermore, single-­
knockout mutants may not exhibit any detectable phenotype as a 
result of gene redundancy. Efforts to characterize these mutants include 
profiling their transcriptome, proteome, metabolome, and phenome 
(2, 3). However, a multiomics approach is unsuitable for studying hy­
pothetical genes on a genome-­wide scale (4). Because our ability to se­
quence genomes outpaces functional characterization, most genes 
are annotated solely based on sequence and structural similarities 
(5). Although new tools such as AlphaFold can provide structural 
insights into cellular functions (6), they have yet to achieve the ac-
curacy needed to replace experimental validations (5). Furthermore, 
having a predicted structure alone does not necessarily clarify func-
tion. For genes annotated by current pipelines, the error rates remain 
relatively high when comparing these annotations with experimental 
data, ranging from 30 to 50% for enzymes and transporters (7). The 
limited understanding of gene function precludes the development 
of pathway-­directed chemical screens (8), which may contribute to 
a largely unexplored area of drug targets. The evolutionary scale 
modeling metagenomic atlas highlights the extensive diversity of 
microbial proteins, underscoring the need to accelerate functional 
genomics research in multiple species (9). For example, the subset of 
hypothetical genes in pathogenic bacteria, such as Streptococcus 
pneumoniae, differs from those in E. coli (10).
One promising approach to revealing gene function is elucidating 
genetic interactions. A genetic interaction occurs when the phenotype 
of a double mutant deviates from expectation based on the phenotypes 
of the two single mutants. A classic example is synthetic lethality, in 
which the individual mutants in two genes have no or minimal fitness 
defects but the double mutant has a severe fitness defect. Because 
genes that form such relationships are often functionally related, we 
can use this information to guide mechanistic studies. Previously, ge-
netic interaction arrays such as genetic interaction analysis technology 
for E. coli (GIANT-coli) (11), cell-envelope genetic interaction map 
(12), and synthetic genetic array (13) were developed to directly quan-
tify the fitness of many double mutants by systematically measuring 
colony sizes or growth in liquid cultures (1, 14). Nevertheless, the pre-
requisites of these approaches include an extensive collection of 
single-­knockout mutants and robotics, which may not be available 
to all researchers. Consequently, a complete genetic interaction array 
is only available in yeast (15). The same requirement applies to CRISPRi 
systems, in which the single-­guide RNAs need to be cloned system-
atically (16, 17). By contrast, transposon insertion sequencing (TIS) 
approaches [e.g., transposon sequencing (Tn-­seq) (18), transposon di-
rected insertion-site sequencing (19), and insertion sequencing (20, 21)] 
assay individual gene knockouts without requiring preconstructed 
single mutants for every gene. Here, a Tn mutant library is generated 
from a strain of choice. The location of Tn insertions and their abun-
dance are determined by next-­generation sequencing of the Tn junc-
tions, and hence fitness of most genes in the genome can be assayed 
in parallel. To discover genetic interactions, the results of a Tn mutant 
library constructed in the wild-­type (WT) background versus a mutant 
background can be compared (22–24). A rate-­limiting step of TIS is 
preparing the DNA library for sequencing the genomic DNA adjacent 
to the Tn insertions. To increase the throughput of TIS, random bar-
code (RB) Tn-­seq was developed by inserting a unique DNA barcode 
within the Tn (25). After associating the insertion sites and barcodes by 
TIS, the linked barcodes serve as a surrogate for mapping and quantify-
ing the Tn mutants through barcode sequencing (BarSeq). Although 
RB Tn-­seq and traditional TIS are powerful for genetic interaction 
studies, they are “one-­to-­all” approaches in which any gene(s) under 
study must first be mutated prior to Tn library construction. By de-
sign, traditional TIS approaches cannot identify two random Tn inser-
tions in a single cell, as these are almost exclusively beyond sequencing 
distance for individual templates.
To overcome these challenges, we developed dual Tn-­seq, which is 
designed for an “all-­to-­all” genome-­wide mining of genetic interactions 
by measuring the fitness of a massive number of double mutants in 
parallel. We chose the human pathogen Streptococcus pneumoniae as 
our prototype as it is naturally competent and genetically tractable (26). 
Briefly, two barcoded Tn libraries were generated in S. pneumoniae 
strain D39W. Genomic DNA was purified from one of the libraries to 
transform the other, generating ~1.4 billion random double mutants. 
To identify and quantify the double mutants, the Tns include an engi-
neered lox site so that the barcodes recombine upon cre induction, 
thus bringing them to within Illumina sequencing distance regardless 
of orientation. We sequenced >10 billion of the fused barcodes and 
determined the fitness of each double mutant by comparing the ex-
pected and actual number of reads and strains, permitting us to sam-
ple ~73% of the total 1.3 million possible double mutant combinations 
across the genome. Our screen identified numerous genetic interac-
tions, many of which were confirmed by independent reconstruction 
of the double mutants. Expectedly, many of these gene pairs are in the 
same or related biochemical pathways, illustrating the power of dual 
Tn-­seq in uncovering gene functions. As a proof of concept, we discov-
ered a new class of cytidine triphosphate (CTP) synthase, a regulator 
controlling peptidoglycan synthesis, factors involved in nucleotide 
transport and amino acid synthesis, and others. Furthermore, we re-
vealed the potential cellular roles of 67 uncharacterized proteins by

identifying their genetic interactions with genes involved in known 
biological processes. Because dual Tn-­seq relies on only a few compo-
nents, it can be readily adapted to elucidate “genetic dark matter” 
across a diverse range of bacterial species.
Results
Design, construction, and validation of barcoded Tn libraries for 
dual Tn-­seq
We constructed two HIMAR1 mariner Tns with spectinomycin or 
erythromycin resistance cassettes (RBloxSpec and RBloxErm), each 
containing sequencing primer binding sites, a lox66 or lox71 site, and 
a 20-­nucleotide (nt) barcode (Fig. 1A). These Tns are designed to 
recombine to produce a dual barcode sequence when cre expression 
is induced. The resulting barcode fusion is irreversible because the 
lox66 and lox71 sites will generate a nonfunctional lox72 site after 
recombination (27). To avoid polar effects, our Tns do not include a ter-
minator that blocks the transcription of an operon. This design also 
enables us to study phenotypes resulting from the overexpression of 
downstream genes.
Transposition is expected to occur in random orientations across 
the genome. However, the lox sites are directional during recombina-
tion. We reason that if the lox sites in the Tns are placed as shown 
in Fig. 1A, the barcodes will be fused regardless of their initial orienta-
tion. Upon cre induction, the chromosome between the insertions will 
either be excised or inverted, depending on the orientation of the two 
Tns (Fig. 1A and fig. S1), resulting in barcode fusion. To demonstrate 
this, we constructed two strains in which RBloxSpec was inserted at 
the penicillin-­binding protein 1b (pbp1b or spd_1925), followed by 
introducing RBloxErm at penicillin-­binding protein 1a (pbp1a or 
spd_0336) in either orientation. Although pbp1a and pbp1b are 493 kb 
apart, we readily detected barcode fusion in cells harboring both 
RBlox-­Tns in either orientation when cre was induced (fig. S2, A to C). 
One concern is that the basal expression level of cre may lead to growth 
defects in the double mutant because it may excise or invert the chro-
mosome. However, we did not detect differences in the growth rates of 
the ∆pbp1a ∆pbp1b mutants in the presence or absence of the cre ex­
pression cassette (PZn-­cre) (fig. S2D), suggesting that the slower growth 
in the ∆pbp1a ∆pbp1b mutant was solely due to the inactivation of 
penicillin-­binding proteins. We conclude that the Cre-­lox system can 
recombine the genome to specifically fuse the barcodes inserted in 
various chromosomal locations and orientations.

lion and 8.8 million unique barcodes for RBloxSpec and RBloxErm, 
respectively. Plasmids purified from each pooled library were mixed 
with MarC9 transposase and genomic DNA of S. pneumoniae for in vitro 
transposition. After end-­repairing and purification, the transposed

DNA was introduced into the prototype pneumococcal strain D39W, 
harboring an inducible cre.
The Tn insertions and the associated barcodes of each pool were se­
quenced and mapped (fig. S3A), revealing hundreds of thousands of 
insertions with unique barcodes in each library (see methods). Col­
lectively, these libraries covered insertions within the open reading 
frames in ~1600 of the 1914 protein-­coding genes of the pneumococcal 
genome. As a proof of concept, we sought to recapitulate known syn-
thetic lethal relationships between pbp1a and pbp2a (spd_1821) and 
pbp1a and macP (spd_0876) (28–30) using the barcoded libraries. To 
do this, we transformed the WT and ∆pbp1a strains with the RBloxErm 
library and sequenced the barcodes in the transformants (fig. S3B). 
As expected, there were fewer Tn insertions in pbp2a or macP when 
the library was transformed into the ∆pbp1a background compared 
with the wild type (fig. S3C). Additionally, insertions in pbp1a were 
markedly reduced when we transformed the RBloxErm library into 
∆pbp2a and ∆macP mutants (fig. S3C), indicating that the Bar-­seq ap­
proach can reproduce results from traditional Tn-­seq screens.
Dual Tn-­seq identifies genetic interactions in S. pneumoniae
Under standard laboratory growth conditions, S. pneumoniae has 
~1600 nonessential genes (17, 18, 31). Theoretically, at least 1.3 million 
combinations of double mutants can be generated. To approach satura-
tion of our screen, we first optimized the transformation protocol 
(fig. S4, A and B). Next, we transformed the RBloxErm library with DNA 
purified from the RBloxSpec library, resulting in ~1.4 billion double 
mutants (Fig. 1B). The double mutants were plated on blood agar plates 
supplemented with spectinomycin and erythromycin. After overnight 
incubation, colonies were resuspended in culture media, pooled, and 
allowed to recover for two hours (~1 doubling) before cre induction. 
Cells were further incubated for 2 hours before harvesting. Quantitative 
PCR (qPCR) revealed that barcode recombination had reached satura-
tion by this time point (fig. S4C). Genomic DNA was extracted and 
dual barcodes were amplified and sequenced. More than 10 billion 
reads were generated, with 3.1 billion reads having barcode pairs that 
both mapped to an open reading frame (ORF).
We used two metrics to identify pairs of genes with significant ge-
netic interactions, both negative interactions (covering both synthetic 
lethality in which the double mutant is completely lethal and “syn-
thetic sick” in which the double mutant is less fit but still viable) and 
positive interactions (fig. S5). The first metric, “readRatio,” is calcu-
lated by dividing the number of observed dual-­barcode reads for a 
given gene pair by the expected number, determined through a proba-
bilistic model from the abundances of individual gene barcodes. The 
second metric, “zStrains,” uses the expected number of double mutant 
strains from unique barcode combinations as the mean of a Poisson 
distribution to describe the distance, in standard deviations, of the ob­
served number of strains from expectation. These metrics are affected 
globally and uniformly by the location and distance between the two 
Tn insertions across the chromosome (fig. S6), allowing us to correct 
this bias mathematically. Moreover, gene pairs with too few reads or that 
are too close to each other were filtered (see methods). To better visual-
ize putative genetic interactions, we plotted the readRatios against the 
zStrains for the entire dataset (Fig. 1C and table S1). As expected, our 
positive control gene pairs pbp1a and pbp2a, as well as pbp1a and 
pbp1b, exhibited strong negative genetic interactions (Fig. 1, D and E, 
and fig. S2D) (28). We could not detect the known synthetic lethal pair 
pbp1a and macP, likely because of the small size of the macP gene, 
which resulted in insufficient coverage. In total, 958,696 nonessential 
gene pairs (73%) have adequate coverage, which can be used for mining 
genetic interactions.
Next, we sought to empirically determine the readRatio and zStrains 
values that represent bona fide negative genetic interactions, includ-
ing both synthetic lethal and synthetic sick interactions. We selected 
107 gene combinations spanning a wide range of these metrics and 
asked whether we could construct these double mutants by transform-
ing a knockout construct of one gene into the corresponding deletion 
background (fig. S7, A and B). With a stringent threshold of a 100-­fold 
reduction of transformation efficiency in our assay, we found 15 syn-
thetic lethal gene pairs from this list (fig. S7, C and D, and table S2). 
Six double mutants formed small colonies on the plates (fig. S7E), 
suggesting they are synthetically sick. When double mutants were 
nonviable, their corresponding gene pairs exhibited lower values of 
zStrains and readRatio (fig. S7, F and G). We next grew 31 of the vi-
able double mutants and found 15 that exhibited growth defects in 
liquid cultures to various degrees (figs. S7G, S8, and S9). The mini-
mum model for genetic interactions was employed (32), which states 
that double mutants should grow identically to the least-­fit single 
mutant, assuming no genetic interaction. Consistently, many double 
mutants followed this pattern and were deemed noninteracting 
(fig. S9). We define two thresholds for negative genetic interactions 
using functional relatedness and a shuffle test (see methods), which 
gave false discovery rates of 7 and 4% for the medium (zStrains ≤ 
−3.0, readRatio ≤ 0.2) and strong (medium thresholds and zStrains ≤ 
−4.0 or readRatio ≤ 0.05) genetic interactions, respectively (Fig. 1C). 
Here, we define the medium thresholds as inclusive of the “strong” 
category. The medium threshold covers most gene pairs that exhib-
ited growth defects during the validation step (28 out of 36; 77.8% hit 
rate, or 22.2% false positive rate). Because we prioritized novel genetic 
interactions for validation, the actual false positive rate may differ from 
that obtained by sampling the entire dataset. In total, 244 genetic 
interactions satisfied the medium threshold (fig. S10 and table S3), 
excluding an enrichment of genes surrounding the origin (see supple-
mental text). Our strict thresholds may not include all true interac-
tions, but others could be detected by inspecting the interaction 
profiles of known genes (fig. S11 to S13, supplemental text).
Next, we compared the sensitivity of dual Tn-­seq to that of RB Tn-­seq 
in individual mutants. To accomplish this, 71 knockout mutants were 
constructed by disrupting the genes of interest with RBlox Tns. We 
then performed individual RB Tn-­seq in these strains and compared the 
number of interactions identified. Because RB Tn-­seq was performed 
once in each mutant, we controlled for genes with recurring low fitness 
values by calculating a new metric termed fitnessmedian, defined as the 
log2 relative abundance of mutants in a gene relative to the median 
abundance in other backgrounds. Out of 104,961 interactions exam-
ined using RB TnSeq, 57 genetic interactions were above the detection 
limits (|fitnessmedian| ≥ 3, |t| ≥ 5) (Fig. 2A and table S4) (25), giving a 
hit rate of ~0.04%. By comparison, the hit rate of dual Tn-­seq is 0.025% 
(244 of 958,696). Thus, we estimate the sensitivity of dual Tn-­seq to 
be ~65% of RB Tn-­seq, which equates to the expected overall coverage 
(73%). Overall, the double mutant fitnesses measured by RB Tn-­seq 
and dual Tn-­seq correlate (Fig. 2, B to E). Among the validated gene pairs 
examined by both techniques, double mutants with severe phenotypes 
(synthetic lethal) had lower fitnessmedian values than those that exhib-
ited growth defects only in the liquid medium (Fig. 2, F and G). By 
contrast, pairs identified by dual Tn-­seq that had moderate growth 
defects often showed minimal defects in RB Tn-­seq (Fig. 2, F and G), 
possibly due to differences in the outgrowth procedures for the two 
assays (Fig. 1B and fig. S3B).
Genetic interactions uncovered by dual Tn-­seq reveals functions  
of hypothetical genes
We conducted a clusters of orthologous groups (COG) analysis on the 
identified genetic interactions. The largest group of interactions in-
volves genes of unknown function (Fig. 3A). Although many of these 
79 interactions involve two unknown genes, 67 contain an annotated 
gene that aids in clarifying their functions (Fig. 3B). Many genes often 
have a genetic interacting partner that belongs to the same COG 
(Fig. 3B), suggesting that the cells produce many redundant systems 
for acquiring or producing essential resources (supplemental text).

For example, we found that three genes (spd_0751, spd_0752, and 
spd_0753) have strong negative interactions with genes encoding the 
glutamate/glutamine ABC transporter GlnPQ (spd_1098-­spd_1099) and 
the oligopeptide transporter Ami (spd_1667-­spd_1671) (fig. S13, C to E). 
Consistently, simultaneous deletion of amiE and spd_0751 resulted in a 
small colony phenotype (fig. S7C). Spd_0753 is annotated as pyrrolidone-­
carboxylate peptidase, a widespread peptidase that cleaves L-­pyroglutamyl 
residues at the N terminus of peptides (33), whereas Spd_0751 and 
Spd_0752 are uncharacterized membrane proteins containing DUF969 
and DUF979 domains, respectively. Foldseek searches suggest that 
Spd_0751 has remote homology with phosphotransferase system trans-
porters and arsenate pumps, whereas Spd_0752 resembles a gluconate 
permease. The negative genetic interactions among ami, glnP, and 
spd_0751-­0753 suggest that these collectively support amino acid acquisi-
tion (fig. S13, D and E), especially glutamate and/or glutamine. Many 
bacteria synthesize glutamate and glutamine from the Krebs cycle inter-
mediate ɑ-­ketoglutarate, but because S. pneumoniae lacks the Krebs 
cycle, it is auxotrophic for these amino acids (34, 35). However, it main-
tains the enzyme (GdhA, Spd_1158) that converts ɑ-­ketoglutarate to glu-
tamate, suggesting that it can salvage exogenous ɑ-­ketoglutarate (fig. S13C). 
As expected, gdhA has a negative genetic interaction with the glutamine 
synthase gene glnA (spd_0448) (fig. S13D). Thus, we speculate that 
spd_0751-­spd_0753 is an alternative peptide transport system or an ɑ-­
ketoglutarate importer. Consistently, spd_0751-­spd_0753 expression 
increases in a ∆glnA ∆glnP double mutant (36).
We observe an enrichment of interactions in genes associated with 
the transport and metabolism of amino acids, inorganic ions, and nts 
(Fig. 3A). Although these genes account for ~21% of all genes in the 
genome, they represent 33% of all identified interacting partners. As 
expected, we detected many interactions between salvage genes and 
their corresponding de novo biosynthetic pathways as well as between 
redundant transporters. Notably, dual Tn-­seq provides strong evidence 
for the identity and substrates of transporters with vague database 
annotations (e.g., spd_1422 and spd_0411-­0412) (fig. S12, C and D, and 
fig. S13, A and B). Additional discussions and examples are provided 
in the supplemental text, including the putative roles for some other 
genes of unknown function (e.g., spd_1794, fig. S14).
The DUF1846 protein Spd_0310 is an ammonia-­dependent 
CTP synthase
We identified a strong negative interaction between pyrG (spd_0442) 
and spd_0310 (COG4868) (Fig. 4, A and B). PyrG is the only known CTP 
synthase in all life forms (37, 38), producing CTP by amination of uridine 
triphosphate (UTP) using L-­glutamine as the preferred amine donor 
(Fig. 4C) (39). Spd_0310 contains a DUF1846 domain and has been 
linked to iron homeostasis and virulence, though its molecular function 
remains unknown (40). We confirmed this genetic interaction by placing 
spd_0310 under a zinc-­inducible promoter and depleting in a ∆pyrG 
background (NUS4797; ∆spd_0310 ∆pyrG // PZn-­spd_0310), resulting 
in a significant growth defect (Fig. 4, D and E). To test whether spd_0310 
participates in CTP biosynthesis or salvage, we examined whether ex-
ogenous cytidine could rescue the growth defect in NUS4797. Indeed, 
cytidine supplementation corrected the defect, although adding other 
nucleosides did not (Fig. 4E and fig. S15, A and B).
Next, we performed RB Tn-­seq in NUS4797 to identify mutations 
that suppress the lethality of ∆spd_0310 ∆pyrG. When spd_0310 was 
depleted in a ∆pyrG background, there was an increase in insertions 
upstream of pnrABCD and spd_1425. PnrABCD is a nucleoside trans-
porter (41), although Spd_1425 is an uncharacterized major facilitator 
superfamily transporter. Notably, the insertions are enriched only in 
the same orientation as the transcription of pnrABCD and spd_1425 
(Fig. 4, F and G). As the Tn lacks a terminator, the Tn insertions likely lead 
to the overexpression of these downstream transporters. Expectedly, 
overexpression of spd_1425 alleviates the growth defects (Fig. 4D), 
suggesting that both transporters are involved in nucleoside import. 
In support of this, we observed that knocking out both ∆spd_1425 and 
∆pnrABCD exacerbates the phenotype of ∆pyrG upon spd_0310 deple-
tion (fig. S15C) and abolishes cytidine uptake, as judged by the lack of 
rescue when adding exogenous cytidine (fig. S15D). The screen also 
revealed two other mutations that could suppress the ∆spd_0310 ∆pyrG 
interaction: knockouts of the pur-­operon repressor purR (spd_1776) and 
the stringent response gene relA (spd_1458) (Fig. 4, H and I). PurR is 
implicated in controlling purine/pyrimidine biosynthesis and uptake 
(39, 42) and thus ∆purR may increase the pool of CTP in the cell. By 
contrast, RelA induces the stringent response by synthesizing the alar-
mone (p)ppGpp. Because (p)ppGpp is an anti-­​inducer of PurR (43), a 
relA mutation will increase the nt pools by derepressing PurR.
To assay for cytidine uptake in our mutants, we monitored their 
growth after supplementing with the toxic analog 5-­fluorocytidine (5FC) 
(44). The ∆purR, ∆relA, and spd_1425 overexpression mutants showed 
reduced growth with 5FC compared with the wild type (fig. S15E), con-
firming increased salvage. Mutants lacking spd_1425 but not pnrABCD 
displayed considerably reduced 5FC sensitivity (fig. S15E), suggesting 
that Spd_1425 is the primary cytidine transporter in S. pneumoniae. 
Combining ∆spd_1425 ∆pnrABCD with ∆pyrG or ∆spd_0310 did not 
affect 5FC sensitivity as both triple mutants behaved similarly to the 
parent strains (Fig. 4J). These findings strongly suggest that Spd_0310 is 
involved in CTP synthesis rather than nucleoside salvage. Thus, we pu­
rified Spd_0310 and demonstrated that it is indeed a bonafide CTP syn-
thase, capable of converting UTP to CTP using ammonia exclusively as the 
nitrogen donor (Fig. 4K and fig. S16, A and B). Given its role as an alter-
native CTP synthase, we renamed spd_0310 as pyrJ.
YjbK is a putative activator of the cell wall biosynthesis protein MurA
S. pneumoniae harbors two UDP-­N-­acetylglucosamine 1-­carboxyvinyl­transferases, 
MurA (Spd_1764) and MurZ (Spd_0967). Both catalyze the condensa-
tion of UDP-­GlcNAc with phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) for peptidogly-
can biosynthesis (Fig. 5A) (45). Cells lacking both genes are nonviable 
(45). Unlike in most bacteria, MurZ appears to be the predominate 
ortholog in S. pneumoniae (46). Dual Tn-­seq revealed a strong negative 
interaction between the uncharacterized gene yjbK (spd_0981; 
COG4116) and murZ, but not murA (Fig. 5, B and C), suggesting that 
YjbK is a regulatory factor specifically for MurA.
YjbK belongs to the CYTH superfamily, which is found across all do-
mains of life (47). YjbK has a triphosphate tunnel metalloenzyme fold that 
is thought to bind triphosphorylated substrates but lacks an HFxxxxExExK 
motif required for nucleotidyl cyclase activity (48). In general, the 
biochemical activities of CYTH superfamily proteins remain unknown 
(48). Depleting MurZ, but not MurA, caused the cells to deform and lyse 
in a ∆yjbK back­ground (Fig. 5, D to F), indicating that peptidoglycan 
synthesis was inhibited. A RB TnSeq screen revealed insertions that 
presumably lead to the overexpression of murA or murC (spd_1349) 
as well as the inactivation of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (Ppc, 
Spd_0953), which could alleviate the growth defect caused by ∆yjbK 
and murZ depletion (Fig. 5, G to I), consistent with reduced MurA activity. 
MurC in­stalls the first L-­alanine residue to UDP-­MurNAc, the product 
of MurA/MurZ and MurB, whereas Ppc (Spd_0953) converts PEP, a sub-
strate of MurA, to oxaloacetate (Fig. 5A). Thus, ∆ppc is expected to in-
crease MurA ac­tivity. We confirmed that ectopic expression of murA, 
murC, and yjbK, as well as ∆ppc, rescued the synthetic lethality of murZ 
and yjbK (Fig. 5, J and K). We conclude that YjbK is likely required for 
MurA function. This model explains why ∆yjbK is attenuated (49) as it 
reduces peptidoglycan synthesis. Whether YjbK modulates MurA activ-
ity by direct protein-­protein interactions or indirectly by influencing 
substrate availability remains to be determined.
Discussion
A deeper understanding of gene function is required to find new strate-
gies for combating the rising problem of antimicrobial resistance (50).

offered an unprecedented opportunity for functional genomics, as it 
enables high-­throughput methods to link genotypes with phenotypes 
(51). A growing body of work underpins the power of identifying gene 
interactions in studying gene function. For example, RodZ was discov-
ered by isolating mutants that can grow only in conditions in which 
the elongasome is dispensable (52). Other examples include the iden-
tification of the lipoteichoic acid ligase TacL (53, 54), the capsule length 
control factor CpsCD (55), lipoproteins that control cell wall synthesis 
(56, 57), and the cell division regulator KhpAB (58). Here, we report 
dual Tn-­seq, which combines RB Tn-­seq with the Cre-­lox system to 
systematically mine genetic interactions. By evaluating the fitness of 
double mutants en masse, we identified new nucleotide metabolic 
genes, uncovered a regulator for cell wall synthesis, and revealed can-
didates involved in central metabolism.
The alternative CTP synthase identified in this study, PyrJ, is mostly 
found in Firmicutes and Actinobacteria (40) (fig. S17). As expected, ~31% 
of genomes harboring a pyrJ homolog lack pyrG (fig. S18), including key 
pathogens such as Clostridium tetani, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, and 
Clostridioides difficile. Consistently, pyrJ was shown to be essential in 
some of these species (59, 60). PyrJ negatively interacts with the gluta-
mine transporter gene glnP (Fig. 4B and fig. S13D), likely because re-
duced glutamine levels result in decreased PyrG activity. Thus, bacteria 
harboring PyrJ may have a competitive advantage when glutamine, but 
not ammonia, is limiting. PyrJ comprises an N-­terminal P-­loop ATPase-­
like domain and a C-­terminal domain with a cytidine deaminase-­like 
fold. We speculate PyrJ emerged by coupling an ATPase with a cytidine 
deaminase, thus powering the reverse reaction by ATP hydrolysis. 
Because cytidine deamination liberates ammonium, this would explain 
why PyrJ has not evolved to accommodate glutamine as a nitrogen donor.
We found that YjbK is required for MurA function. This result may 
explain why overexpression of MurZ, but not MurA, causes aberrant cell 
morphology in S. pneumoniae (46). Although they are maintained at 
similar concentrations, MurZ activity seems to predominate over that 
of MurA (46), suggesting that most MurA may be inactive inside the 
cell. Upon MurZ inactivation, YjbK may correct the defect by mod­ulating 
MurA activity without changing its cellular amount (46). We postulate 
that YjbK is a failsafe mechanism for adjusting MurA activity, either 
directly or indirectly, upon sensing a decrease in MurZ activity. Because 
YjbK homologs are found only in Firmicutes (fig. S19), it is intriguing 
why MurA homologs in other organisms do not require YjbK for function.
Dual Tn-­seq has limitations. For example, the single-­Tn libraries 
have uneven distributions of insertions across the genome, indicating 
insertion hotspots and/or the fitness of single mutants. Crossing 
these Tn libraries amplifies this bias, leading to several abundant double 
mutants that consume considerable sequencing power. Similarly, 
small genes and intergenic regions often have fewer insertions, lead-
ing to their underrepresentation in the libraries. Furthermore, Tn 
mutants with strong growth defects will inherently have little cover-
age because they are eliminated during the initial library generation 
step. As a result, we do not expect dual Tn-­seq to detect many positive 
genetic interactions. In its current state, dual Tn-­seq appears best 
suited to exploring the synthetic lethal landscape in bacteria. We also 
note small blind spots (~6 kb) in which the transformability is reduced 
during double mutant selection, similar to GIANT-­coli, although this 
only affects 0.7% of interactions. Lastly, since the double mutants need 
to be plated at very high density, there may be phenotypic discrepan-
cies upon reconstruction.
Functional genomic approaches to systematically assay genetic in-
teractions in bacteria hold great promise in uncovering hitherto un-
characterized genetic dark matter. Our presented dual Tn-­seq approach 
is one such strategy. Recently, related efforts to assay genetic interac-
tions in bacteria have combined CRISPR interference and TIS to probe 
the interactions between essential gene knockdowns and Tn mutants 
(61), or used CRISPRi strategies to knock down the expression of mul-
tiple genes (62, 63). The CRISPRi-­based approaches have the advantage 
of partial knockdowns, thus permitting the analysis of essential genes, 
with the added burden of generating guide RNA libraries (62, 63). 
Nevertheless, we envision each of these strategies to be advantageous 
for specific bacteria and different questions. Dual Tn-­seq has an ad-
vantage in that TIS methods (including RB TnSeq) have been readily 
applied to many diverse bacteria, so its general implementation should 
be possible. Because we interrogated a bacterial genome with a smaller 
size (~2000 protein-­coding genes), implementation in a bacterium with 
a larger genome will require the construction of more double mutants and 
increased sequencing depth. The latter should not be an issue as sequenc-
ing costs keep dropping. Given this reality, it should also be straightfor-
ward to profile the fitness of dual Tn-­seq double mutant libraries under 
different conditions to identify condition-­specific genetic interactions. As 
such, we envision dual Tn-­seq as an important tool for the high-­resolution 
interrogation of bacterial molecular networks.
Materials and methods
Bacterial strains, plasmids, and growth conditions
The strains used in this study are listed in table S5. Unless otherwise 
specified, S. pneumoniae cells were grown in brain heart infusion 
broth (BHI), tryptic soy broth (TSB), or on tryptic soy agar plates 
supplemented with 5% (vol/vol) sheep blood (blood plates) (Biomed 
Diagnostics, 221261) at 37°C in 5% CO2. E. coli was grown in lysogeny 
broth (LB) for most experiments or in terrific broth for protein expres-
sion. When indicated, antibiotics were added at final concentrations 
of 0.3 μg/mL for erythromycin (Erm), 300 μg/mL for kanamycin 
(Kan), 300 μg/mL for streptomycin (Str), and 200 μg/mL for spectino-
mycin (Spec) for S. pneumoniae. For sublethal growth measurements 
in Spec, 20 μg/ml was used. For E. coli, ampicillin and kanamycin were 
added at final concentrations of 100 μg/mL and 50 μg/mL, respec-
tively. Expression of the czcD promoter (PZn) was induced by adding 
ZnCl2 to a final concentration of 450 μM. To counteract the cell divi-
sion defects caused by Zn2+ toxicity, 45 μM MnCl2 was added to the me­
dium simultaneously (64, 65).
Strain construction and transformation
Primers for generating PCR amplicons are listed in table S6. PCR products 
were synthesized using Phusion DNA polymerase unless otherwise speci-
fied. Genetic cassettes were assembled using Gibson assembly (66). 
Pneumococcal strains were constructed by transforming cells with PCR 
amplicons, assembled fragments, or genomic DNA (gDNA) after inducing 
natural competence, as described previously (67, 68). Briefly, 1 mL of log 
phase culture was incubated with 1 mM CaCl2, 0.04% (w/v) bovine serum 
albumin, and 250 ng of competence-­stimulating peptide (CSP-­1) for 10 min 
at 37°C in 5% CO2. DNA was added, and the cells were incubated for 
1.5 hours at 37°C in 5% CO2 before being plated on blood agar supple-
mented by the indicated antibiotics. Markerless deletion mutants were 
generated using the Janus (P-­kan-­rpsL+) or Sweet Janus (P-­sacB-­kan-­
rpsL+) cassettes with counter-­selections with Str and 5% (w/v) sucrose 
blood agar with or without added ZnCl2 and MnCl2. Plates were incubated overnight at 37°C in 5% CO2 before the cells were harvested for barcode sequencing. The number of 
reads per million of transposon insertions on the positive (forward read-­through) or negative (reverse read-­through) strand was enumerated. The genomic loci of pnrAB (F), 
purR (G), spd_1425 (H), and relA (I) are shown. (J) The indicated strains were grown in BHI at 37°C in 5% CO2 and released into fresh medium (right) or containing 5FC (left) at 
37°C. Growth was monitored by measuring the optical densities of the cultures at 600 nm (OD600) over time. Plotted are the means of three biological replicates and the 
standard deviation. (K) Purified PyrJ (Spd_0310) converted UTP to CTP using ammonia, but not glutamine, as the amine donor. By comparison, PyrG used glutamine or 
ammonia for CTP synthesis. Plotted are the means and standard deviation from three independent experiments.

Measurement of growth and microscopy
For spot dilutions, strains were grown in the indicated media at 37°C in 
5% CO2 until the OD600 was between 0.1 and 0.5. Cultures were diluted 
to an OD600 of 0.05 and ten-­fold serially diluted. Two microliters of 
each dilution were spotted onto blood agar plates with or without added 
ZnCl2/MnCl2. Plates were incubated overnight before imaging. For 
growth curves, strains were grown in the indicated media at 37°C in 5% 
CO2 until the OD600 was between 0.1 and 0.5. Cultures were diluted to 
an OD600 of 0.01 with BHI broth to a final volume of 200 μL before being 
transferred to 96-­well plates. If the cells were grown in broth supple-
mented with ZnCl2/MnCl2, they were washed twice in 1 mL of phosphate-­
buffered saline before being diluted to an OD600 of 0.01 with BHI broth 
to a final volume of 200 μL. Growth measurements were performed by 
incubating the plate in a Tecan Spark 10M microplate reader at 37°C. 
OD600 measurements were taken every 20 min after a short pulse of 
shaking for 20 s. Double mutant validation growth curves were per-
formed by growing cells to an OD600 of 0.1 to 0.5 in BHI, then diluting 
them in either fresh BHI or by first spinning the cells at 8,000 x g for 
2 min, washing once in TSB, and resuspending them in fresh TSB. Cells 
were normalized in their respective medium to a starting OD600 of 
0.01, transferred to 96-­well plates, and incubated at 37°C in 5% CO2. 
Timepoints were taken every 30 min by transferring the plate to a 
Tecan Spark 10M microplate reader, shaking for 20 s, and measuring 
the OD600. For microscopy, cells were added to 1% (w/v) agarose pads 
and imaged using an Olympus IX81 inverted microscope equipped 
with a Hamamatsu C11440 digital camera.
Construction of plasmid vectors comprising the RBlox-­transposons
pZIK244 harboring RBloxSpec was constructed by cloning an amplicon 
comprising the Magellan6 Tn (18) generated with primers O662 and 
O663 using the Zero Blunt TOPO Cloning Kit (Invitrogen). These prim-
ers added the D1/D2 priming sites and the lox71 site to the Tn. The 
barcoded pZIK244 was electroporated into Electromax DH10B cells 
(Invitrogen) following the manufacturer's instructions.
pZIK251 harboring RBloxErm was constructed by cloning a cassette 
comprising a codon-­optimized ermAM (71), U1 and U2 priming sites, 
and the lox66 site. First, we chemically synthesized the cassette (gBlocks, 
IDT) and amplified it with primers O2269/O2270 to add the Mariner 
inverted repeats. The amplicon was cloned using the Zero Blunt TOPO 
Cloning Kit (Invitrogen). The intermediate vector was used as a tem-
plate for PCR with primers O2377 and O2378. The resulting amplicon 
was DpnI-­treated, assembled by Gibson assembly, and transformed 
into NEB 5-­alpha (NEB) cells following the manufacturer’s instructions 
to produce pZIK251.
Barcoded transposon vector pools were generated by PCR amplifica-
tion of plasmids pZIK244 and pZIK251 with primers O930 and O931 
(for pZIK251) or O1078 and O1079 (for pZIK244) that add 20-­nt ran-
dom barcodes and the overlapping regions for Gibson assembly. We 
used 200 ng of template plasmid per PCR to maximize barcode diver-
sity and did 18 (for pZIK244) or 25 (for pZIK251) independent PCRs. 
The reactions were DpnI-­treated, and the amplicons were pooled and gel 
extracted using the Zymoclean Gel DNA Recovery Kit (Zymo Research). 
Purified amplicons were ligated through Gibson assembly, purified using 
the DNA Clean & Concentrator kit (Zymo Research), and electroporated 
into Electromax DH10B cells (Invitrogen) as per manufacturer’s instruc-
tions. The RBloxErm and RBloxSpec plasmid pools have an estimated 
8.8 million and 15.2 million unique barcodes, respectively.
Library construction
The RBloxErm and RBloxSpec plasmid pools were extracted using the 
QIAprep Spin Miniprep Kit (Qiagen). gDNA was extracted from 
NUS1927 [rpsL1 ∆bgaA::t1t2-­PZn-­cre]. Construction of Tn libraries was 
performed as described previously (55) with modifications. In vitro 
transposition was done by mixing 12.5 μL 4x buffer A (100 mM Tris-­HCl 
8.0, 400 mM NaCl, 60 mM MgCl2, 40% (v/v) glycerol, 8.0 mM 1,4 di-
thiothreitol [DTT], and 1.0 mg/mL bovine serum albumin [BSA]), 1.5 μg 
genomic DNA prepared from strain NUS1927, 1.5 μg barcoded RBloxSpec 
or RBloxErm plasmid pool, and 0.14 μg purified MarC9 transposase 
in 50 μL reaction volumes. The mixture was incubated for 1.5 hours at 
30°C and purified using the DNA Clean & Concentrator kit (Zymo Re­
search). Transposed DNA was diluted in water to a final volume of 
25.5 μL, and then 3.3 μL buffer B (0.5 M Tris HCl pH 8.0, 100 mM MgCl2, 
and 10 mM DTT), 1.65 μL of 20 mg/mL BSA, 1.25 μL of 2 mM dNTPs, and 
1.25 μL of T4 DNA polymerase (NEB, M0203L) were added to the DNA 
and incubated for 30 min at room temperature. After incubation, 1.25 μL 
of 2.6 mM NAD+ and 1.25 μL of E. coli DNA ligase (NEB, M0205L) were 
added to the mixture and further incubated at room temperature over-
night. The repaired DNA was transformed into strain NUS1927. Trans­
formants were collected from the plates, pooled, and stored in 15% glycerol 
at −80°C. We constructed two libraries for RBloxSpec, one library 
(ML1) was used to generate 88 million mutants of our dual-­TnSeq library, 
and a second library (ML3) for the remaining 1.33 billion mutants 
(see below).
Transposon library mapping
Tagmentation of gDNA isolated from the RBlox transposon libraries was 
done using the Illumina DNA Prep (M) kit according to the manufac-
turer’s instructions with the following modifications. Tagmented DNA 
was amplified with custom primers O1282 and O2417 (for RBloxErm) 
and O1283 and O1414 (for RBloxSpec). The “post-­tagmentation clean­up” 
step was done to enrich for transposon junctions and add the P7 and 
i7 sequences, using the following thermocycler settings: 68°C for 3 min; 
98°C for 3 min; 25 cycles of 98°C for 45 s, 62°C for 30 s, 68°C for 2 min; 
and lastly 68°C for 1 min. Following the 'clean-­up libraries' steps, P5, 
i5, and read1 sequences were added through amplification of the prod-
uct with O1282 and O1143 for RBloxErm and O1283 and O1144 for 
RBloxSpec using Phusion polymerase and the following settings: 95°C 
for 3 min; 20 cycles of 95°C for 30 s, 60°C for 30 s, 72°C for 1 min; and 
lastly 72°C for 5 min. Amplicons were size-­selected using AMPure XP 
Reagent (Beckman Coulter) at a 0.5x “beads to sample ratio” and se-
quenced through the Illumina platform at Azenta Life Sciences. We 
sequenced four preparations of the ML1 library and three preparations 
of the ML2 and ML3 libraries to increase the number of usable barcodes. 
We also mapped the library two more times using another method 
(25, 72). Briefly, after shearing the DNA purified from the libraries to 
~300 bp, we used the KAPA Hyper Prep Kit to ligate a splinkerette adapter 
(table S6), followed by an initial round of PCR to enrich for transposon 
insertion sites (with oligos Rd1_FOR_tnseqV3_Zik_SpecR and Rd1_
REV_tnseqV3 for the RBloxSpec library, and Rd1_FOR_tnseqV3_Zik_
ErmR and Rd1_REV_tnseqV3 for the RBloxErm library). After Ampure 
bead cleanup, we performed a second round PCR reaction with the 
 alleviated when murA and murC were expressed ectopically or when ppc was inactivated. The indicated strains (table S4) were grown in BHI broth with added ZnCl2 and MnCl2 at

All of the above sequencing reads were combined and mapped using

Dual tn-­seq library construction
To generate the Dual Tn-­seq double-­mutant library, frozen aliquots of 
the RBloxErm library in the NUS1927 background were thawed and 
diluted to an OD600 of 0.05 in BHI. The diluted library was incubated 
for 3 hours at 37°C in 5% CO2. It was further diluted to an OD600 of 
0.1 in BHI and transformed with the gDNA purified from the RBloxSpec 
library. Typically, 200 to 500 ng of gDNA per milliliter of culture was 
used for generating the Dual Tn-­seq libraries. Transformation reactions 
were incubated for 1.5 hours before being plated on blood agar supple-
mented with spectinomycin and erythromycin, and then incubated 
overnight at 37°C in 5% CO2. Transformants were collected, diluted to 
an OD600 of 0.1 in BHI, and incubated for 2 hours at 37°C in 5% CO2. 
ZnCl2 was added to a concentration of 0.85 mM to induce cre, and the 
cells were further incubated for 2 hours to allow recombination of the 
barcodes. Cells were collected by centrifugation at 15,000 x g for 5 min 
at room temperature, the supernatant was discarded, and the pellets 
were frozen at −80°C. We generated 1.42 billion transformants across 
21 batches of independently constructed double-­mutant libraries. The 
first 88 million of these transformants were constructed using the first 
RBloxSpec library (ML1) for donor gDNA, although the remaining used 
the ML3 library.
Cell pellets of the libraries were thawed and heat-­inactivated at 85°C 
for 1 hour. gDNA was then extracted and quantified using the Quant-­iT 
Qubit dsDNA HS Assay Kit (Q32851, ThermoFisher). Because each batch 
of the Dual Tn-­seq library has variable numbers of transformants, we 
normalize the amount of gDNA added to the PCR based on the total 
number of CFUs in the library. PCR amplification was performed using 
Phusion polymerase with the following settings on 300 ng of combined 
gDNA per 50 μL reaction: 95°C for 3 min; 20 cycles of 95°C for 30 s, 55°C 
for 30 s, 72°C for 10 s; and lastly 72°C for 5 min. The primers used incor-
porated P5/P7, i5/i7, and read1/read2 sequences for the Illumina platform 
(O1369 and O1370; O3987 and O1370). Amplicons were sequenced at 
Azenta Life Sciences. Collectively, we amplified and sequenced 21 double-­
mutant libraries across five independent NovaSeq PE150 runs.
Quantitative PCR (qPCR)
To quantify the relative amount of fused barcodes after cre induction, 
we collected ~1 million transformants of the Dual Tn-­seq library. Cells 
were diluted to an OD600 of 0.1 and grown in BHI for 3.5 hours at 37°C 
in 5% CO2 before diluting the culture again to an OD600 of 0.1 in the same 
medium. For each time point, cells were removed and centrifuged for 
5 min at 15,000 x g at room temperature. The supernatant fraction was 
removed, and the pellets were stored at −80°C. Pellets were thawed and 
heat-­inactivated by incubation at 85°C for 45 min. gDNA was extracted 
and quantified by Qubit. qPCR was performed on 1.2 ng of gDNA using 
the FastStart Essential Green Master kit (Roche) and primers O1635 and 
O1636 for the dual-­barcode sequence and O1583 and O1584 for pbp1a. 
Reactions were run on a LightCycler 96 (Roche) with the following set-
tings: 95°C for 10 min; 40 cycles of 95°C for 10 s, 52°C for 10 s, 72°C for 
15 s; and a final melting step of 95°C for 10 s, 65°C for 60 s, 97°C for 1 s. 
Relative abundance was determined by the ΔΔCt method (73) and nor-
malized to the copy number of pbp1a.
Dual Tn-­seq data analysis
PEAR was used to merge Illumina paired-­end reads (74). After extract-
ing pairs of barcodes from each Illumina read, we filtered out pairs in 
which each barcode had been mapped to a genomic location in the rele­
vant RB Tn-­seq library. We found that the distribution of the number 
of reads for each individual strain (pair of barcodes) was highly skewed, 
with a large minority of barcode pairs being observed only once or 
twice. We hypothesized that these rare barcode pairs are due to chi-
meric PCR. To test this, we PCR-­amplified dual-­barcode sequences 
from a pooled culture of 96 double mutants to detect any unexpected 
barcode combinations that were generated from PCR chimeras, using 
template DNA concentrations of 300, 500, and 1000 ng, respectively. 
The frequencies of chimeras were 0.02% (300 ng), 0.3% (500 ng), and 
4% (1,000 ng). Based on these results, we used 300 ng of gDNA per 
reaction to minimize inference by chimeras. Also, we found that bar-
code pairs that correspond to synthetic lethal pairs of genes often had 
very low counts. So, strains were ignored within each run unless they 
had at least 3 to 6 reads, with varying thresholds across runs. Then, 
for each run, we counted the number of strains (i.e., different pairs of 
barcodes) and the total number of reads for each pair of genes. We 
performed two analyses: one using only insertions within the central 
10 to 90% of each gene and another using 0 to 100%. The latter analysis 
increases the number of usable insertions although potentially includ-
ing some non-­disrupting insertions. Because the first run had roughly 
3x fewer strains but similar reads to the rest, we normalized this run 
by dividing the reads by three. Then, we summed the numbers of reads and 
strains across runs. Given the read and strain count for each (directed) 
pair, we estimated the expected numbers of reads or strains based on 
the proportion of reads or strains for each gene. For example, the 
proportion of reads for each gene pair will be:
f1 = reads for gene 1 / total
f2 = reads for gene 2 / total
f12 = f1*f2
expected12 = f12 * total reads
We then combined the actual and expected reads (or strains) in both 
directions to get statistics for undirected pairs. (In our data tables for 
undirected pairs, we always use locusId1 < locusId2.) We then adjusted 
these read and strain numbers for chromosomal position. Specifically, 
we divided the pneumococcal chromosome into 30 bins. For each pair 
of bins, we computed the median read ratio (actual reads / expected 
reads) and the median strain ratio (fig. S6A). The median read ratio 
within each bin ranged from 0.24 to 2.9, and the median strain ratio 
within each bin ranged from 0.46 to 1.72. The enriched pairs of regions 
are near each other on the chromosome, especially near the origin or 
terminus of replication, or combine the origin and the terminus. These 
may indicate regions of the chromosome that are physically near each 
other, which might increase the efficiency of Cre-­lox recombination. 
Given the estimated biases due to chromosomal location, we multi-
plied the original estimate of the expected number of reads or strains 
by the bias and then computed the final (adjusted) read ratio and 
zStrains = (strains -­ expected strains) / sqrt(expected strains) (fig. S5). 
We required at least five expected double mutant strains for each gene 
pair to achieve sufficient coverage. Otherwise, the gene pairs were 
discarded. Similarly, insertions in close proximity (within 6 kb) were 
ignored, as these are selected against upon double selection (fig. S6B). 
All plots included in the figures report values from the analysis using 
insertions found within 10 to 90% of the gene. In total, 802,114 and 
958,696 pairs had sufficient coverage to allow the possibility of achiev-
ing a significance value of zStrains ≤ −3 for the 10 to 90% and 0 to 
100% gene analyses, respectively. For double mutants with sufficient 
coverage in the 10 to 90% analysis, the median number of strains per 
gene combination was 45, and the median read count per gene com-
bination was 527.
Code to analyze Illumina reads from Dual Tn-­seq experiments is 
available from the bitbucket feba repository (https://bitbucket.org/
berkeleylab/feba), Dryad (https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.7d7wm3840), 
and Figshare (76). BarcodePairs.pl identifies pairs of barcodes in a fastq 
file, combineBarCodePairs.pl combines the output of barcodePairs.pl

Estimating the false discovery rate of negative genetic interactions
To choose thresholds for zStrains and readRatio, we first shuffled the 
pairs of insertions identified by Dual Tn-­seq to eliminate any genuine 
genetic interactions. Due to variation in coverage based on position 
in the chromosome, for each pair, we randomly selected a new location 
for each insertion among the insertions in that library within the same 
bin (30th of the chromosome). The number of reads for each strain 
was kept the same. Given the actual data set, the shuffled data set, and 
thresholds for zStrains and readRatio, we estimated a false discovery 
rate by dividing the number of genetic interactions in the shuffled data 
set by the number in the actual data. Each threshold was applied to 
an analysis considering only central insertions (within 10 to 90% of 
each gene) and to another analysis encompassing all insertions within 
each gene (0 to 100%); these two results were then combined.
We initially chose zStrains ≤ −3 and readRatio ≤ 0.2, which we refer 
to as medium confidence (Fig. 1C). At these thresholds, the actual data 
contained 533 putative negative interactions, whereas the shuffled 
data contained 17, resulting in a false discovery rate of 17/533 = 3%. 
However, upon examining the putative interactions, we realized that 
for the majority of them, at least one of the genes was near the origin 
of replication (spd_2033-­spd_2069 and spd_0001-­spd_0006), which 
seemed questionable. We tested five pairs that met these thresholds, 
and none were found to be synthetic lethal or produce small colonies. 
When we conducted growth curves for four pairs, we observed reductions 
in growth rates for three out of the four pairs. However, none of the three 
confirmed pairs (spd_0006 with spd_0677, spd_0703, or spd_0767) 
showed a clear functional relationship. We decided to exclude interac-
tions involving the origin. After removing these, 244 putative negative 
interactions remained in the actual data, compared to 16 in the shuf-
fled data, leading to a false discovery rate of 7%. To identify putative 
strong negative interactions, we required zStrains ≤ −3 and readRatio ≤ 
0.2, along with either zStrains ≤ −4 or readRatio ≤ 0.05 (Fig. 1C). After 
excluding the region around the origin, we identified 111 strong nega-
tive interactions in the actual data (before shuffling), while the shuffled 
data set yielded 4, resulting in an estimated false discovery rate of 
4/111 = 4%. Within the medium thresholds, we found that 28 out of 
36 pairs validated (14 synthetic lethal, 5 small colony, and 9 growth de-
fects; table S3), giving us an estimate of the positive rate of 28/36 = 
77.8%. Note that we prioritized interactions that were not functionally 
obvious for follow-­up studies; therefore, this number is likely a con-
servative estimate of the actual positivity rate.
As another way to test the putative genetic interactions, we consid-
ered their functional relatedness by using COG function codes. After 
removing proteins that did not belong to a COG or were assigned codes 
R or S (for “general function prediction only” or “function unknown”), 
we were left with 168 pairs among the medium-­confidence interactions. 
Among these pairs, 71 (42%) had overlapping COG function codes or 
demonstrated functional similarity confirmed in this study. However, 
among the high-­confidence interactions, this rose to 65%, which was 
significantly higher (p = 0.0016, Fisher’s exact test). For comparison, 
among all 34 non-­origin pairs with validated genetic interactions (re-
gardless of whether they met either threshold for Dual Tn-­seq), the rate 
of functional similarity was 66%, which is similar to the rate of 65% for 
the strong hits. This confirms that many of the strong hits are genuine.
RB Tn-­seq analysis and BarSeq
Cultures of the indicated strains were grown until they reached the log 
phase (when the OD600 is between 0.1 to 0.5). They were transformed with 
300 to 500 ng of gDNA purified from either the RBloxErm or RBloxSpec 
library and plated with appropriate antibiotics and ZnCl2 and MnCl2 
as indicated. Typically, at least 1 million transformants will be ob-
tained. Cells were collected by flooding the plates with BHI, scraping 
the cells with a spreader, and pooling them into a collection tube. Cells 
were stored at −80°C after adding glycerol to a final concentration of 
15% (vol/vol). To estimate the sensitivity of Dual Tn-­seq (Fig. 2), we 
performed single RB Tn-­seq on 71 deletion mutants. We prioritized 
genes involved in strong or multiple genetic interactions as identified 
from Dual Tn-­seq and those constructed during the validation experi-
ments (fig. S7). For isolating suppressors, transformants were plated 
on blood agar plates without added ZnCl2 and MnCl2 and incubated 
overnight at 37°C in 5% CO2. Barcodes were amplified from 300 ng of 
gDNA purified from the surviving colonies using Phusion polymerase 
and the Illumina-­ready primers listed in table S6. RBloxErm barcodes 
were amplified with primers O1143 and O1370 using the following 
thermocycler settings: 95°C for 3 min; 20 cycles of 95°C for 30 s, 52°C 
for 30 s, 72°C for 10 s; and finally 72°C for 5 min. RBloxSpec barcodes 
were amplified with O1144 and one of twelve differentially indexed 
reverse primers (table S6) using the following settings: 98°C for 5 min; 
25 cycles of 98°C for 30 s, 60°C for 30 s, 72°C for 10 s; and finally 72°C 
for 5 min. Amplicons were gel-­purified and sequenced through the 
Illumina platform at Azenta Life Sciences. Insertions were quantified 
using Perl scripts described previously (25).
To compare the relative abundance of mutations in each gene to what 
we would expect in the absence of biological effects, we used data from 
control mutants. For RBloxSpec mutants, the control was a mutant of 
spd_1726, which encodes pneumolysin (pneumolysin targets cholesterol-­
containing membranes and is not expected to affect the physiology of 
fitness of S. pneumoniae during growth in vitro). For RBloxErm mutants, 
the control was a mutant of spd_0562 (bgaA), which encodes a beta-­
galactosidase and is commonly used as an ectopic locus for genetic ma-
nipulation. Given the barcode counts for an experimental sample and a 
control sample, we computed gene fitness values (estimated log2 changes 
in the abundance of mutants of each gene) and t-­like test statistics, as 
described previously (25). These analyses are based on the central 10 to 
90% of each gene. We considered |t| ≥ 5 as a significant effect. In some 
cases, we identified recurring low fitness for a gene, regardless of the 
mutant background in which the experiment was conducted. So, we 
computed fitnessmedian of a gene in a mutant background as the log2 
relative abundance of mutants in that gene, relative to the median 
relative abundance in other mutant backgrounds. Besides the require-
ment for |t| ≥ 5, we also required |fitnessmedian| ≥ 3 to identify genetic 
interactions.
After construction, we noticed that a majority of cells in our RBloxTn 
libraries were unencapsulated (colony morphology, Quellung reaction). 
Therefore, for more accurate comparisons with Dual Tn-­seq selection 
pressure, we removed the capsule locus (spd_0312-­spd_0333) from plots 
in Fig. 2A-­C. Similarly, since our control mutant had an insertion in 
spd_1726, we also removed spd_1726-­spd_1728 from these plots, since 
we tended to see an “enrichment” of insertions here in other back-
grounds. Fig. 2D and E had genes around the origin removed due to a 
high rate of presumed false-­positives (see supplementary text). RB Tn-­seq 
metrics that could be scored twice (from transforming two different 
backgrounds [i.e., the reverse]) were averaged.
Measuring transformation efficiencies
Single mutants containing an RBloxSpec or RBloxErm cassette were 
constructed as described above. These strains served as the template 
for the PCR. In general, amplicons that span 800 bp upstream and 
downstream of the RBloxSpec cassette were synthesized using Phusion 
polymerase with primers listed in table S6. Amplicons were purified 
using the QIAquick PCR Purification Kit (Qiagen) before being trans-
formed into recipient cells harboring RBloxErm after inducing natural 
competence. Briefly, 1 mL of recipient cells was diluted to an OD600 of 
0.05, transformed with 20 to 45 ng of the amplicon, and placed using

appropriate antibiotics. The amount of each amplicon and the recipi-
ent cultures were kept consistent for each experiment. The number of 
transformants was quantified as colony-­forming units per milliliter. 
Transformation efficiency was calculated using CFU/mL using the equa-
