Ideally, a chemogenomic screening set will repre­
sent a balanced distribution of targets across the human 
proteome. In reality, libraries reflect the availability of 
chemical probes for certain targets; that is, probes that are 
available commercially and/or present in large screening 
files in pharmaceutical companies and research institutes. 
As a result, initiatives such as those led by the Structural 
Genomics Consortium (SGC) aim to create collections of 
selective chemical probes that populate gene families (for 
example, inhibitors of kinases, bromodomain-containing 
proteins and methyltransferases) in a more unbiased way. 
Such novel probe collections are particularly useful for 
the creation of chemogenomic libraries23,24.
An important consideration in the use of a che­
mogenomic library is that the annotated target of 
a small-molecule screening hit might not be the one 
responsible for perturbing the observed phenotype. This 
problem is mitigated to some extent by library designs 
that include multiple structurally diverse compounds for 
the same annotated ‘on‑target’. This important design 
feature takes into account the fact that small-molecule 
tools are inherently likely to exhibit some degree of 
off-target pharmacology, potentially including targets 
that are yet to be characterized and/or are not avail­
able for screening in standard panels. Furthermore, 
phenotypic screens are often initially conducted at con­
centrations (for example, micromolar concentrations) 
at which even (apparently) highly potent and selective 
tools may have relevant off-target effects. Although 
such an approach is not ‘fail safe’, as structurally diverse 
compounds with common on‑target activity could also 
have common (maybe unknown) colinear off-targets, 
it nonetheless enables the generation of much stronger 
target–phenotype hypotheses than could be achieved 
from single hits alone. In addition, the use of analogous 
negative control compounds that are structurally similar 
to the active tools but are devoid of substantial activity 
against the annotated target14 can also prove very useful 
to support follow‑up target validation efforts and can 
help to rule out misassignments.
Even when the annotated target itself is subsequently 
ruled out, it may still provide clues about the relevant 
target and thus guide focused follow‑up experiments, 
including target validation using other technologies 
(for example, RNAi and CRISPR–Cas9)25. Furthermore, 
unbiased functional genomic profiling across the broader 
gene family to which the initial annotated target belongs 
may also be worthwhile, as the (unknown) off-target 
activity of a small molecule could well be associated with 
a closely related protein.

true kinase coverage is considerably higher owing to polypharmacology (156 kinases are inhibited by more than 50% at 
a concentration of 100 nM by at least 1 compound)43.

Multiparameter 
optimizations
Algorithms that allow several 
variables to be balanced and 
assessed on the basis of their 
importance relative to the 
specified objective.
Pan-assay interference 
compounds
(PAINs). Compounds that often 
appear as false-positive hits in 
screens owing to promiscuous 
binding, fluorescence, redox 
activity or metal chelation 
effects.
Careful consideration should be given to the concen­
tration chosen for screening the library. If possible, a full 
dose–response curve should be generated for the entire 
set, but this is very much dependent on the throughput 
of the assay. In addition, in our experience, phenotypic 
screens in human primary cells can often yield hits with 
bell-shaped dose–response curves (for example, cell 
viability may become compromised at higher concen­
trations, leading to an apparent reduction in the assay 
signal)26. Screening at a single high concentration (as 
one might for a target-based approach) may, therefore, 
lead to a preponderance of false negatives, and impor­
tant mechanistic information could be lost. Cell viability 
assays should, therefore, be run in parallel to the pheno­
typic screen in the same cell-based system to enable early 
assessment of therapeutic indices. Due to issues of poly­
pharmacology at high compound concentrations, single-­
point screens should be carried out at concentrations 
that are commensurate with the potency and selectivity 
of the molecules in the set. Chemogenomic screening 
may also yield false-positive hits that result from effects 
such as compound fluorescence and luciferase reporter 
binding27. Simultaneous screening for these effects in the 
same cell-based system as that used for the phenotypic 
assay can efficiently ‘weed out’ false positives18 (FIG. 1).
Examples of chemogenomic libraries
We have outlined some of the important features of che­
mogenomic library development and described general 
considerations regarding the successful use of the sets in 
phenotypic screening efforts. A number of chemogenomic 
libraries have been reported in the literature, and although 
details regarding the selection criteria used for compound 
inclusion in the sets are somewhat lacking, the gene fam­
ily and target coverage of the libraries are described. As 
a result, the differences between the libraries, and their 
potential merits and limitations, are apparent.
The Pfizer chemogenomic library. To create the Pfizer 
chemogenomic library, millions of compounds and their 
associated screening data points (of which there were 
billions) were mined using bioinformatics, and mole­
cules were selected for further analysis if they achieved 
potency against their primary annotated target at a con­
centration of less than 500 nM. Tailored multiparameter 
optimizations28 were developed for key druggable gene 
families in order to select the most appropriate phar­
macological modulator of a particular target (FIG. 2a,b). 
Key features of this selection process included a num­
ber of parameters that ensured the appropriateness of 
a compound for cell-based screening, such as selectiv­
ity, permeability, solubility and cytotoxicity (predictive 
algorithms were used if these values were not available). 
Compounds were not included if they had promiscuous 
activity that resulted from ‘false-positive’ pharmacology 
(so‑called pan-assay interference compounds (PAINs)29) 
or if they were predicted to be frequent hitters using 
chemical-­fingerprint-based Bayesian models30.
Another important aspect in the design of the Pfizer 
chemogenomic library was the selection, where available, 
of different chemical templates with the same annotated 
on‑target pharmacology, as the inclusion of these in the 
library would provide more confidence that the putative 
target arising from a phenotypic screen represents a real 
hit. Finally, human curation was used to ensure that every 
molecule selected for the set was appropriate.
The Pfizer chemogenomic library has been screened 
extensively by Pfizer and by external collaborators within 
a short period of time, and the results of these efforts 
will be reported individually in due course. To illustrate 
just one recent example, the library was screened in a 
muscleblind-like protein 1 (MBNL1)-upregulation assay 
to discover new leads for the treatment of myotonic 
dystrophy type 1. For the first time, small molecules were 
identified that upregulated MBNL1 (the screen was per­
formed at 1 μM concentration with a 3.3% hit rate). Hits 
included several histone deacetylase inhibitors, suggesting 
that MBNL1 is epigenetically regulated31.
The Sigma-Aldrich Library of Pharmacologically 
Active Compounds. The Sigma-Aldrich Library of 
Pharmacologically Active Compounds (LOPAC1280) 
contains 1,280 pharmacologically relevant small­
molecule agents, and a complete list of compounds 
and their annotated targets is available from the sup­
plier. The composition of the screening set reflects the 
most commonly screened targets in drug discovery 
(FIG. 2c; TABLE 1). For instance, GPCRs are the targets for 
approximately 60% of the drugs on the market, and more 
than 50% of the compounds in LOPAC1280 target GPCRs. 
LOPAC1280 is thus well suited to screens in which GPCR 
biology is known to be associated with the phenotypic 
effects under investigation. However, no further details 
have been published regarding the criteria that were 
used to select compounds for inclusion in this library. 
Presumably because of its commercial availability, 
LOPAC1280 has been extensively screened in a variety of 
cell-based phenotypic assays (there are more than 100 
publications referenced in PubMed), and some exam­
ples of the considerable value that this set has brought to 
chemical biology research are described below.
Chemogenomic libraries can be used to highlight new 
targets for which marketed drugs already exist, but as the 
LOPAC1280 set contains marketed drugs, they can also 
directly link existing drugs to new indications. However, 
collections that contain approved drugs — such as the 
Prestwick Chemical Library32,33, for which small mole­
cules were selected on the basis of their known bioavail­
ability and safety in humans — could also be used for the 
latter purpose (TABLE 1). Drugs are not always necessarily 
designed or selected for their exquisite selectivity, and 
therefore, hits from chemogenomic libraries that contain 
a large number of nonselective drugs may suffer from 
polypharmacological phenotypic effects that complicate 
target deconvolution.
The GlaxoSmithKline Biologically Diverse Compound 
Set. The GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) Biologically Diverse 
Compound Set (BDCS) library contains nearly 6,000 
compounds that were chosen for their coverage of 
diverse biological activities according to external and 
GSK biodata sources34 (FIG. 2d; TABLE 1). Computer scripts

were written in order to analyse millions of screening 
data records, and this analysis resulted in the selection 
of compounds for the library, which contains drugs that 
target 736 unique proteins in total. Priority was given 
to the selection of molecules with high selectivity, par­
ticularly against off-targets within the same gene family. 
Another important feature of the selection process was to 
choose up to 10 molecules for each target to provide con­
fidence in a target if multiple tool compounds showed 
activity. The compounds were stored as stock solutions 
in dimethyl sulfoxide, and source plates were prepared 
using acoustic dispensing technology, which also ena­
bles the selection of specific compounds if desired35. No 
further details regarding the selection criteria for the 
inclusion of compounds in the BDCS library were pro­
vided, but it is noticeable that the library is dominated 
by GPCR (27%) and kinase (22%) targets, which reflects 
the prominence of these targets in drug discovery efforts 
within the pharmaceutical industry. Interestingly, the 
coverage of ion channel targets and nuclear receptors in 
the BDCS library seems to be considerably lower than 
that of the Pfizer chemogenomic library.
The Mechanism Interrogation PlatE library. The 
Mechanism Interrogation PlatE (MIPE) library was devel­
oped by the National Center for Advancing Translational 
Sciences (NCATS) at the US National Institutes of Health 
(NIH). Version 3.0 contains 465 small molecules (most 
of which seem to be commercially available) and focuses 
on oncology targets; it includes 73 approved drugs, 168 
clinical candidates and 207 preclinical candidates, and 
covers 39 well-defined mechanisms of action36,37. As the 
compounds in the MIPE library are advanced preclin­
ical or clinical agents, for which extensive safety data 
is available, the set is particularly well-suited to drug 
repositioning efforts.

High-content
A term used in this Review to 
describe a cell-based assay 
that measures several 
parameters, often using 
automated imaging analysis.
Annotated gene families represented in the MIPE 
library include kinases (209), GPCRs (26) and ion chan­
nels (16). The broad cellular mechanisms of compounds 
in the set include modulators of nuclear receptor tran­
scription factors (28), metabolite conversion (23), lipid 
metabolism (18), histone epigenetic machinery (16) and 
apoptosis (15). Although there is considerable breadth in 
the cellular pathways that are represented in the library, 
it is understandably dominated by kinase inhibitors, 
given the prominent role of these drugs in the treatment 
of cancer38.
A more recent library developed at NCATS (MIPE 
version 4.0) contains an expanded list of 1,912 agents and 
was built using the same principles as those applied to the 
creation of version 3.0 (C. Thomas, personal communi­
cation). The library was created from a mixture of com­
mercial and private sources, and is regularly updated with 
emerging probe molecules from the literature and novel 
agents that are entering the clinic. To date, it has been 
screened in more than 300 cancer lines and more than 
100 other phenotypic assays, reflecting the considerable 
utility of the library.
Molecular Libraries Program Probes (NIH). Although 
not a chemogenomic screening library as such, the 
decade-long collective contributions to the Molecular 
Libraries Program (MLP) probe set, which is supported 
by the NIH, created 375 small molecules that cover 
a diverse range of biological targets, including major 
families such as kinases, GPCRs and hydrolases, but 
also relatively underexplored targets such as GTPases 
and RNA-binding proteins. In several instances, MLP 
chemical probes were developed for certain biological 
targets for the first time. Several vignettes were recently 
described in which MLP probes enabled the explo­
ration of biological pathways and therapeutic hypo­
theses39. Notable successes include the development of 
numerous serine hydrolase inhibitors, subtype selective 
sphingosine‑­1‑phosphate receptor modulators and 
allosteric modulators of muscarinic receptors.
All bioassay data associated with MLP probes have 
been made freely available through the BioAssay Research 
Database (BARD), which allows researchers to mine and 
visualize screening data40. However, as for any chemical 
probe, caution should be exercised when considering the 
selectivity, and hence the target annotation, of the small 
molecule in the set. A recent publication described the 
use of polypharmacology prediction software to cor­
rectly identify off-targets of several MLP probes that were 
distantly related to their primary annotated targets41.
The Protein Kinase Inhibitor Set (GSK and SGC). The 
Protein Kinase Inhibitor Set (PKIS) contains 367 pro­
tein kinase inhibitors that were selected from more than 
3,000 molecules previously published by scientists at 
GSK42. Key criteria in selecting probes included com­
pound availability (more than 5 mg had to be available), 
broad coverage of the kinome and chemotype diversity 
to aid target deconvolution from phenotypic screens. As 
such, this library represents a chemogenomic gene fam­
ily subset that should enable more focused screening of 
compounds targeting kinases. Bioassay data were initially 
reported for individual compounds in the set in more 
than 60 publications, but they were then consolidated and 
made readily available at ChEMBL. The selectivity of the 
entire library was recently comprehensively characterized 
in 224 kinase assays and 24 GPCR assays43. This effort 
led to the identification of new selective inhibitors for 
previously untargeted kinases and the appreciation that 
some kinase inhibitor templates crossreact with GPCRs. 
The PKIS was also profiled in a luciferase inhibition 
assay counter-screen, in which 6% of the library showed 
activity20, highlighting potential false-positive issues that 
should be assessed and included in the annotation of 
chemogenomic libraries more broadly.
Importantly, the PKIS library is now freely available for 
public screening efforts and has been profiled in a diverse 
array of assays spanning multiple therapeutic areas. At the 
time of writing, more than two dozen publications have 
described the successful use of the PKIS, and access to the 
set has helped to secure a substantial amount of public 
funding (W. Zuercher, personal communication).
Applications of chemogenomic library screening
Target identification. The chemogenomic libraries 
described above have enabled biological targets and 
molecular mechanisms to be linked to a number of 
important phenotypic effects in a variety of cell types. For 
example, LOPAC1280 was screened in a high-content 3D 
imaging assay of lymphangiogenic sprouting, a process 
that has a key role in cancer metastasis and organ trans­
plant rejection44. Among the hits (drugs were screened 
at a concentration of 5 μM, and there was a 2.8% hit rate) 
was mevastatin, and subsequent screening of other stat­
ins suggested that the major target of this class of drugs, 
3‑hydroxy‑3‑methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase 
(HMGCR), may have a key role in lymphangiogenesis.
The BDCS library was screened in a high-content 
imaging phenotypic assay that measured histone tri­
methylation specifically trimethylation of histone 3 
lysine 27 (H3K27me3), a chromatin mark that is associ­
ated with several tumours) to explore the mechanisms 
that modify this oncogenic post-translational modifica­
tion (drugs were screened at a concentration of 5 μM, 
and there was an 8.5% hit rate)34. The identification of 
8 out of 8 previously reported EZH2 methyltransferase 
inhibitors as hits in the screen served as a useful pos­
itive control for the assay. The screen also identified 
non-methyltransferase and non-demethylase targets as 
potential upstream regulators of H3K27me3, and the 
Ingenuity Pathway Analysis tool highlighted a number 
of pathways that were potentially involved in this pro­
cess, including ERBB2–ERBB3 and pancreatic adeno­
carcinoma signalling, among other pathways. However, 
it should be noted that the majority of targets identified 
in the screen only had one chemical probe per target.
In isolation, it is unlikely that small-molecule chem­
ical probes will directly reveal novel therapeutic targets. 
Their true utility lies in the ease with which new (poten­
tially druggable) targets and pathways may be identified 
through small-molecule screening. Small-molecule 
chemical probes can provide clues about the targets

Perturbagens
Modalities — such as genetic 
reagents (for example, short 
interfering RNA and short 
hairpin RNA), small molecules, 
proteins or peptides — that 
alter the phenotype of a cell in 
some way.
involved in controlling a particular phenotype, thus 
focusing subsequent knockdown or knock‑in experi­
ments, which tend to be more technically challenging. 
Therefore, chemogenomic screening hits contribute to 
a ‘body‑of‑evidence’ approach to target identification 
when used in conjunction with other chemical and 
molecular biology validation techniques. By way of illus­
tration, LOPAC1280 was also screened in a high-content 
imaging assay to discover new mechanisms that inhibit 
the formation of cancer cell protrusions called invado­
podia, which are involved in tissue invasion and matrix 
remodelling (drugs were screened at a concentration 
of 10 μM, and there was a 0.4% hit rate)19. The promis­
cuous cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) inhibitor pur­
valanol A45 and another molecule annotated in the set as 
a CDK family inhibitor (GCP74514A) were identified as 
hits in the assay. Although many CDKs are involved in 
cell cycle regulation, the weak cell cycle arrest activity of 
purvalanol A suggested that the potential target of this 
compound was CDK5, which is not involved in cell cycle 
control. CDK5 was validated as the relevant target using 
CDK5‑targeted RNAi, which achieved inhibition of inv­
adopodia formation in human cancer cells. Interestingly, 
other CDK inhibitors in the LOPAC1280 set had been 
removed from the original hit list owing to irreproduci­
bility that probably arose from cytotoxicity or edge effects 
in the screening plate (that is, artefacts potentially caused 
by thermal gradients in peripheral wells). These observa­
tions emphasize the need to carefully interrogate the data 
from such screens and take into account the possibility of 
false-negative results.
Similarly, the MIPE library (version 3.0) was recently 
used in conjunction with short interfering RNA (siRNA) 
screening that targeted genes in the druggable genome 
to identify new therapeutic targets for neuroblastoma36. 
In particular, a common target, Aurora B kinase, was 
identified using both approaches as a suitable candidate 
for further research. This work demonstrates the value 
of simultaneous chemogenomic and genetic screening 
approaches to expedite target identification.
Another recent approach integrated genomic screen­
ing (using CRISPR–Cas9 and RNAi to induce loss of 
function) with chemogenomic screening to identify 
new potential therapeutic targets in a rare sarcoma46. 
The Broad Institute Informer Set (which contains 
72 drugs that are approved by the US Food and Drug 
Administration (FDA), 100 clinical candidates and 268 
biologically active chemical probes) was screened for 
antiproliferative effects in a cell line derived from the sar­
coma. Among the hits were compounds targeting CDK4 
and XPO1 (also known as exportin 1), which concurred 
with hits from the genomic screens, and further target 
validation revealed these genes as potential therapeutic 
targets for the sarcoma under investigation. In broader 
profiling experiments, the sensitivities of hundreds of 
cancer cell lines to the Broad Institute Informer Set have 
been assessed; such studies have identified associations 
between activating mutations in the oncogene CTNNB1 
(which encodes β‑catenin) and sensitivity to BCL‑2 
antagonism47, and links between KRAS mutations and 
neuroblastoma48.
Drug repurposing. In some instances, chemogenomic 
screening is able to reveal new uses for existing drugs. 
This can be indirect, when target or pathway hits are 
coincidently modulated by clinical agents, or direct, 
when the drugs themselves are hits in the phenotypic 
screen. For example, PKIS screening in multiple cell 
line models of the rare cancer chordoma helped to 
define a therapeutic hypothesis regarding inhibition of 
epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) that is cur­
rently being tested in clinical trials49. Such findings can 
considerably accelerate the drug discovery process, as 
compounds in chemogenomic libraries can be directly 
tested in animal models or clinical efficacy experiments. 
However, consideration should be given to the possibil­
ity that the required dose (free-drug exposure) and the 
therapeutic index of the drug in the new indication may 
differ from those in the original indication.
A repurposing opportunity was identified by screen­
ing LOPAC1280 in patient-derived leukaemia cells for 
cytotoxicity or antiproliferative activities (drugs were 
screened at a concentration of 10 μM, and there was a 2% 
hit rate)50. Quinacrine (an antimalarial drug developed 
in the 1920s) showed antitumour activity that presum­
ably derives from its ability to intercalate into dou­
ble-stranded DNA in a manner that reverses leukaemia 
gene expression. The study also used a counter-screen in 
peripheral blood mononuclear cells from healthy donors 
to be able to select hit molecules or mechanisms that 
were selectively toxic to leukaemia cells.
The MIPE 3.0 library was screened for small mole­
cules that could promote destabilization of an oncogenic 
mutant form of the GTPase KRAS (KRAS‑G12V) in 
HeLa cells; this screen identified compounds that pro­
moted the loss of KRAS‑G12V (REF. 51). Among the six 
hits annotated in the library as ABL kinase inhibitors, 
only ponatinib, nilotinib and DCC‑2036 (also known as 
rebastinib) reduced the levels of KRAS‑G12V, suggesting 
that off-targets of these drugs were responsible for the 
observed phenotypic effect. These studies also highlight 
a limitation regarding the selectivity of small-molecule 
perturbagens and emphasize the need to take poly­
pharmacology into account when generating mecha­
nistic hypotheses. For example, ponatinib decreased 
KRAS‑G12V levels by approximately 40% when used 
at a concentration of 1 μM, and it is known to inhibit 
57 wild-type kinases with a half-maximal inhibitory 
concentration of less than 1 μM (REF. 52).
Combinatorial chemogenomic library screening with 
existing drugs may also reveal novel synergistic therapeu­
tic opportunities. The MIPE 3.0 library was also screened 
in combination with ibrutinib, an inhibitor of Bruton’s 
tyrosine kinase, to identify new therapeutically relevant 
drug combinations for the treatment of diffuse large B 
cell lymphoma (DLBCL)53. Ibrutinib had synergistic 
effects with several phosphoinositide 3‑kinase (PI3K) 
pathway inhibitors (including agents that target the 
ATP-binding site of PI3K and the mechanistic target of 
rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1)), in line with previous 
reports that constitutive PI3K signalling in DLBCL cells 
supports their viability. This work also revealed strong 
cooperativity between ibrutinib and inhibitors of the

Pharmacogenomic
A term that refers to the study 
of how genetics can alter 
responses to drugs.
BCL‑2 family, and the ex vivo treatment of cells from 
patients receiving ibrutinib with the selective BCL‑2 
antagonist ABT‑199 demonstrated the potential clini­
cal utility of this combination in chronic lymphocytic 
leukaemia54. Similarly, a combination screen of ruxol­
itinib (an inhibitor of Janus kinase 1 (JAK1) and JAK2) 
with the MIPE 4.0 library identified additional efficacy 
with ABT‑263 (an inhibitor of BCL‑2 and BCL‑XL (also 
known as BAD)) in the setting of Hodgkin lymphoma55.
An impressive pharmacogenomic interaction landscape 
analysis was also recently carried out to correlate can­
cer-driven alterations with sensitivity to 265 drugs in 1,001 
cell lines56. This approach identified both known and novel 
gene–drug associations, an example of the latter being the 
sensitivity of U2AF1 mutations to FLT3 inhibitors. This 
work will serve as a useful resource for investigating 
further pharmacogenomic interactions in cancer.
Predictive toxicology. Another emerging application 
of chemogenomic screening is the classification of the 
toxic mechanisms of new compounds. For example, 
the BioMAP system comprises a panel of primary human 
cell types that can detect a broad range of toxic mecha­
nisms using an array of different endpoints57. Screening 
of molecules with known mechanisms defined signatures 
in these assays that allow new molecules to be screened 
and compared against the reference database using com­
putational predictive methods. Using this approach, 
a pharmaceutical compound was correctly predicted 
to be a mitogen-activated protein kinase inhibitor with 
a toxicity profile suggestive of skin rash, a side effect 
that was actually observed in clinical trials of this com­
pound58. Therefore, profiling such libraries to provide 
functional ‘fingerprints’ can predict the mechanisms 
of action of new molecules discovered in phenotypic 
screens (in a ‘guilt by association’ manner).
The Library of Network-Based Cellular Signatures 
(LINCS) Program is a large-scale NIH-administrated 
effort to measure the molecular and cellular signatures 
produced by a variety of perturbagens, including small 
molecules. The aim of LINCS is to correlate cellular phe­
notypes with proteomic or transcriptional signatures, 
and make predictions that lead to mechanistic informa­
tion regarding the perturbation. For example, the Broad 
Institute has developed the L1000 gene expression assay59 
that enabled profiling of approximately 1,000 transcripts 
in cells treated with more than 30,000 small molecules 
(including a large panel of FDA-approved drugs and drugs 
with known bioactivities). Associations were then made 
between the gene expression data and known adverse 
drug reactions: that is, harmful or unpleasant side effects 
resulting from drug treatment60. Machine learning meth­
ods were then used to predict potential adverse drug reac­
tions for a large number of investigational drugs and other 
molecules that were profiled in the LINCS L1000 project, 
and these data are available on a useful web portal: Side 
effect prediction based on L1000 data.
High-content and in vivo screening. Advances in 
high-throughput, high-content and multiparamet­
ric imaging assays have proven utility in mechanistic 
elucidation61,62. In one recent report, LOPAC1280 was 
screened in 12 isogenic knockout cell lines with muta­
tions representative of important oncogenic path­
ways63. Following cell staining with Hoechst 33342 (to 
label nuclei) and phalloidin labelled with tetramethyl­
rhodamine isothiocyanate (to visualize actin), 20 fea­
tures of cell morphology were measured. This allowed 
gene–drug interactions to be effectively profiled, creat­
ing a resource termed the Pharmacogenetic Phenome 
Compendium. Through this work, new molecular 
modes of action and opportunities for drug repurposing 
were discovered.
Higher-throughput chemogenomic library screening 
in vivo (for example, in zebrafish and Xenopus tadpoles) 
has also provided new opportunities for a number of 
indications. Due to the parallels between primordial 
line development in zebrafish and cancer metastasis, 
a phenotypic zebrafish screen was developed to iden­
tify small-molecule inhibitors of lateral line migration, 
which is a model of metastasis. Through chemogenomic 
screening, a number of SRC kinase inhibitors were 
found to induce the desired phenotype in zebrafish, 
and importantly, these small molecules also inhibited 
tumour metastasis in mice64. CRISPR–Cas9 mutagenesis 
in zebrafish was then used to validate SRC as an impor­
tant target in cell migration64. A phenotypic screen of 
the LOPAC1280 set in tadpoles found new mechanisms 
that are involved in the development of the lymphatic 
and blood vascular system65. One hit, an adenosine 
A1 receptor antagonist, also blocked vascular endothe­
lial growth factor A (VEGFA)-induced neovasculariza­
tion in mice, and this study demonstrated opportunities 
to identify new mechanisms involved in cancer metasta­
sis65. Another example of in vivo chemogenomic screen­
ing described the use of the Prestwick chemical library to 
identify small molecules that restore muscle architecture 
in a zebrafish model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy66. 
For example, through this work a number of inhibitors 
of the phosphodiesterases (PDEs; including PDE5) were 
shown to improve the muscle phenotype in zebrafish, 
which is in line with observations that PDE5 inhibitors 
exert a beneficial effect in mouse models of the disease67.
The in vivo studies described above also highlight 
the need to consider the possibility of false-negative 
results, as many molecules will not be able to engage 
their respective targets in vivo owing to poor absorption 
and/or nonspecific binding, thus reducing free-drug lev­
els in the organism14. It is also possible that active metab­
olites are responsible for the phenotypic perturbation, 
thus complicating mechanistic elucidation.
Novel on‑target pharmacology. Focused screening 
of a chemogenomic subset library has been shown to 
reveal novel pharmacological mechanisms within the 
same gene family. For instance, in an effort to identify 
novel inhibitors of TAK1 (also known as MAP3K7) for 
the treatment of inflammatory conditions, a biochemi­
cal screen of a kinase-targeted library was carried out68. 
This work led to the identification of TAK1 inhibitors 
that had been shown previously to inhibit p38 in the 
inactive, ‘DFG-out’ conformation69, thus suggesting

for the first time that TAK1 was amenable to this mode 
of inhibition, a hypothesis that was subsequently con­
firmed by X‑ray crystallography. In addition, Bristol-
Myers Squibb recently screened a collection of 7,908 
molecules with known kinase selectivity from existing 
kinase programmes in an interleukin‑23 receptor signal 
transduction assay70. This work led to the identification 
of compounds that bound to the pseudokinase domain 
of tyrosine kinase 2, thus stabilizing its autoinhibitory 
interaction with the catalytic domain.
Broadly, unanticipated on‑target pharmacology 
should be an important consideration when using che­
mogenomic phenotypic screening to facilitate down­
stream mechanism-of‑action studies. For instance, 
certain ATP-site kinase inhibitors have been shown to 
cause on‑target degradation by reducing the recruit­
ment of heat shock protein 90 (HSP90) and its cochap­
erone CDC37, an effect that can be readily overlooked71. 
Other examples include hepatitis C virus inhibitor-
triggered relocalization of nonstructural protein 5A to 
lipid droplets72 and transcription factor degradation by 
immune-modulating drugs73,74. These observations con­
firm the need to develop assays that are reflective of the 
entire range of functional pharmacologies that could 
lead to a particular phenotypic perturbation.
Small-molecule enhancers of alternative modalities. 
Other therapeutic modalities — such as RNAi, gene ther­
apy and gene-editing approaches — could potentially be 
augmented through the co‑administration of small mol­
ecules, and chemogenomic screening provides a means 
to discover novel mechanisms and repurposing opportu­
nities for synergistic combinations. A reporter gene assay 
(the superfolder GFP-Nanog system) was developed to 
identify small-molecule modulators of CRISPR–Cas9 
genome editing75. Chemogenomic screening of nearly 
4,000 small molecules with known biological activities, 
including those in the LOPAC1280 set, led to the iden­
tification of brefeldin A (a protein transport inhibitor) 
and L755507 (a β3 adrenoceptor agonist) as enhancers of 
homology-directed repair75.
In addition, LOPAC1280 screening identified gua­
nabenz (an antihypertensive drug and adrenergic ago­
nist) as an enhancer of siRNA internalization and target 
mRNA silencing by hydrophobically modified siRNA76. 
The mechanism by which guanabenz influenced siRNA 
fidelity was not fully elucidated, although it was sug­
gested that interactions between the positively charged 
protonated drug and the negatively charged RNA form 
nanoaggregates that could have a role in facilitating cel­
lular delivery. These studies illustrate proof of principle 
for small-molecule-enhanced knockdown methodolo­
gies that may provide future therapeutic opportunities.
Another example of this application is the recent 
screening of more than 2,000 FDA-approved drugs for 
their ability to enhance adeno-associated virus gene 
delivery, with the aim of lowering the therapeutic dose 
of the viral vector (and thus potentially avoiding host 
immune stimulation)77. In this study, 13 compounds 
were found to enhance transduction efficiency, although 
their mechanisms of action were not elucidated. Future 
efforts using chemogenomic libraries could reveal new 
targets and pathways linked to the potentiation of vector 
transduction.
Conclusions and outlook
Phenotypic and pathway screening approaches are 
experiencing a renaissance within the pharmaceuti­
cal industry, driven by the prospect of improved drug 
success in phase II trials after the use of assays that are 
more representative of human disease3,4. These assays 
often use primary cells, tissue and/or induced pluripo­
tent stem cells from patients and have potential to bet­
ter represent human disease in a preclinical setting (that 
is, providing a ‘disease-in‑a‑dish’ model)78. Although 
functional genomic methods work well with engineered 
cell lines, it can be challenging to use these approaches 
with more-sensitive primary cells, particularly in 
a high-throughput manner. By contrast, small-molecule 
pharmacological probes are simple and convenient to 
use in cell-based assay and tissue systems.
Chemogenomic screening not only augments coor­
dinated strategies to convert phenotypic screening pro­
jects into target-based drug discovery but also provides 
new opportunities to repurpose existing drugs into 
new indications. Although the chemogenomic libraries 
described above no doubt differ considerably in their 
content, there are general features that are common to 
the creation of each library. These include the need 
to broadly cover biological space with selective pharma­
cological agents79 and the desire to have multiple, struc­
turally distinct chemotypes that have affinity against 
a particular target that can provide confidence in target 
hits. The chemogenomic library criteria outlined in this 
Review could facilitate the creation and application of 
new screening subsets, and possibly the enhancement 
of existing ones.
However, there are several challenges facing both the 
incorporation of chemogenomic screening approaches 
into drug discovery and the subsequent mechanistic 
deconvolution of library hits. Improvements should be 
made in the accuracy of annotation of bioassay data; 
misannotations, both in public and private data repos­
itories, create major issues regarding chemical biology 
database curation and hence selection of the optimal 
pharmacological modulator for inclusion in a che­
mogenomic library21. Initiatives such as Standards for 
Reporting Enzymology Data (STRENDA)80 and the 
BioAssay Research Database (BARD)40 project help to 
standardize the reporting and use of biological activ­
ity data, which will lead to more robust database cura­
tion. Pharmacological databases should then be used to 
ensure that the most appropriate chemical probes are 
selected for inclusion in a chemogenomic library. The 
International Union of Basic and Clinical Pharmacology 
(IUPHAR) and the British Pharmacological Society 
(BPS) have created a portal (the IUPHAR/BPS Guide 
to PHARMACOLOGY), which includes a database 
with highly curated pharmacological information and 
is a particularly relevant chemogenomic resource81. In 
addition, computational protocols that integrate com­
pound–target–pathway and disease information, such

Target occupancy
The interaction between a 
chemical probe or drug and 
its target, resulting in a 
biological response.
as those reported recently by the Innovative Medicines 
Initiative Open Pharmacological Concept Triple Store 
(PHACTS) Project82, can aid in the generation of mech­
anistic hypotheses from chemogenomic hits in pheno­
typic screens. The Open PHACTS protocols also select 
from the IUPHAR/BPS Guide to PHARMACOLOGY 
to identify additional pharmacological agents for target 
validation follow‑up experiments.
The reproducibility of pharmacological screening is 
an important area of consideration for any phenotypic 
and cell-based screening effort, and appropriate statisti­
cal analysis may help to contextualize any variability. The 
reproducibility of pharmacogenomic profiling of cancer 
cell lines was addressed recently, and differences in cell 
seeding density and even the media used in the screen can 
contribute to variability between studies83. By systemati­
cally analysing the potential causes of screening variation, 
consistent results may be obtained, which is essential for 
building confidence in the relevance of a chemogenomic 
target hit. The quantitative interdependence of the four 
pillars of target validation using chemical probes — expo­
sure at the site of action (free-drug levels), quantification 
of target occupancy, expression of functional pharma­
cology and proof of a relevant phenotypic perturbation 
— may also provide insights into differences in the per­
formance of pharmacological agents in different studies14.
Many reported pharmacological probes, which can 
sometimes be included in chemogenomic libraries, carry 
very broad off-target activity. This recognition has led to 
increased community focus on the use of higher-quality 
chemical probes, and the recent creation of The Chemical 
Probes Portal will aid researchers in selecting compounds 
for cell-based and in vivo studies79. In addition, industry–
academia consortia should be fostered to develop selective 
chemical probes against novel (unannotated) targets (one 
successful example being the SGC)84. Chemogenomic 
libraries are, understandably, biased towards the drug­
gable genome. Therefore, hits arising in a phenotypic 
screen could accelerate a target-­based drug discovery 
project, but of course, there are many gene families and 
biological targets that are yet to be drugged or for which 
selective probes have yet to be developed. Target hits in 
a chemogenomic screen may also be statistically under­
powered owing to the lack of structurally differentiated 
pharmacological agents that modulate the identified tar­
gets. For these reasons, chemogenomic library screening 
should ideally be carried out in parallel to unbiased RNAi 
or CRISPR–Cas9 whole-genome screening to maximize 
target and pathway coverage. Other issues facing small-
molecule phenotypic screening efforts include the inevita­
ble occurrence of false-positive results (through compound 
fluorescence, luciferase reporter binding, PAINs, and so 
on) and false-negative results (through low solubility or 
permeability, and bell-shaped dose–response or cytotoxic­
ity curves). Computational techniques must be fully lever­
aged in the selection of probes for a chemogenomic library 
to remove those with predicted physico-biochemical 
characteristics that are undesirable. Bioinformatics and 
pathway analyses of screening data can also address these 
issues. As discussed, counter-screening is essential to mit­
igate problems arising from false-negative or false-positive 
results. Automated methods may be developed to prior­
itize the selection of tool compounds from large chemical 
biology databases for inclusion in chemogenomic librar­
ies. A recent approach assigned a tool score to probes on 
the basis of a computational summary of potency and 
selectivity, which ranked compounds for a particular 
biological target85.
Despite these challenges, we anticipate a substantial 
increase in the use of chemogenomic library screens in 
the years ahead. This is also an area that is ripe for col­
laborative partnerships between academic institutions 
and pharmaceutical companies, bringing together the 
unique assays often found in academia with the well-
curated chemogenomic libraries that may arise from dec­
ades of small-molecule screening in an industrial setting. 
Arguably, chemogenomic libraries created in industry that 
leverage the scale of their small-molecule collections and 
associated data using bioinformatics are well suited to seed 
drug discovery collaborations with academic institutions 
that have developed complex disease-relevant phenotypic 
screens, but where the assay throughput often does not 
support high-throughput screening of millions of mole­
cules. In instances in which high-throughput phenotypic 
assays are viable, chemogenomic libraries could dominate 
such large screening campaigns to expedite the discovery 
of new targets using high-quality molecules that represent 
hundreds-to‑thousands of druggable genes.
In addition, the development of ‘open innovation’ 
chemogenomic libraries that assemble the best availa­
ble reported pharmacological probes can also be antic­
ipated. Although the challenge of target deconvolution 
from a phenotypic screen is not to be underestimated, 
it is clear that the use of well-designed chemog­
enomic libraries can considerably accelerate this pro­
cess. Indeed, chemogenomic approaches can serve as 
a bridge between disease-relevant phenotypic screening 
and the identification of well-defined molecular targets, 
thus enabling all aspects of drug design and develop­
ment. In this manner, chemogenomic screening is likely 
to prove to be an increasingly mainstream approach in 
helping to bring innovative new therapies to patients.

===== Lenski2017_ISMEJ_ExperimentalEvolution-LTEE =====

WINOGRADSKY REVIEW
Experimental evolution and the dynamics of
adaptation and genome evolution in microbial
populations
Richard E Lenski1,2,3
1Department of Microbiology and Molecular Genetics, Michigan State University, East Lansing, MI, USA;
2Graduate Program in Ecology, Evolutionary Biology and Behavior, Michigan State University, East Lansing,
MI, USA and 3BEACON Center for the Study of Evolution in Action, Michigan State University, East Lansing,
MI, USA
Evolution is an on-going process, and it can be studied experimentally in organisms with rapid
generations. My team has maintained 12 populations of Escherichia coli in a simple laboratory
environment for 425 years and 60 000 generations. We have quantified the dynamics of adaptation by
natural selection, seen some of the populations diverge into stably coexisting ecotypes, described
changes in the bacteria’s mutation rate, observed the new ability to exploit a previously untapped
carbon source, characterized the dynamics of genome evolution and used parallel evolution to
identify the genetic targets of selection. I discuss what the future might hold for this particular
experiment, briefly highlight some other microbial evolution experiments and suggest how the fields
of experimental evolution and microbial ecology might intersect going forward.
The ISME Journal (2017) 11, 2181–2194; doi:10.1038/ismej.2017.69; published online 16 May 2017
The distinction between ‘ecological time’ and
‘evolutionary time’ is artificial and misleading.
Changes of both kinds may be on any time scale:
frequently genetic and ecological changes are
simultaneous—Janis Antonovics (1976).
Introduction
Evolution is often viewed as an inexorably slow
process, one that happens over extremely long
periods. By contrast, ecology is typically seen as
occurring much faster, reflecting both the intrinsic
dynamics of biotic interactions and the increasingly
pervasive effects of anthropogenic environmental
change. In fact, however, evolution is simply the
conjunction of ecology and genetics, which involve a
few basic processes—births, deaths, competition,
mutation and selection—that have been happening
since life began and will continue for as long as life
exists.
On-going evolution has been studied in such
organisms as finches in the Galapagos archipelago
(Grant and Grant, 2014) and fruit flies in the
laboratory (Burke et al., 2010). But nowhere is
evolution in action more apparent than in micro-
organisms. Examples include such striking and
impactful changes as antibiotic resistance in bacteria
and altered host-range in viruses, as well as subtle
changes that allow the spread of pathogens to be
tracked by epidemiologists or that produce microbes
slightly better adapted to their environments than
their predecessors.
In this review, I will focus mostly on an experi-
mental study in which a single bacterial species has
been evolving under constant conditions for many
years. Such ‘pure culture’ studies have sometimes
been criticized because they eliminate the richness
and complexity of the natural world. I cannot
dispute that point. However, science often pro-
gresses by simplifying nature in order to probe and
make sense of more tractable systems. Moreover, one
of the most striking outcomes of the experiment has
been the richness and complexity that have emerged.
The long-term evolution experiment
Structure of the experiment and motivating questions
The long-term evolution experiment, or LTEE, is
simple both conceptually and practically. Twelve
populations were started the same ancestral strain of
Escherichia coli in 1988. The ancestral strain has no
plasmids or functional prophages, and E. coli is not
naturally transformable, so there is no horizontal
gene
transfer.
However,
each
population
has

Molecular
Genetics,
Michigan
State
University,
Biomedical
Physical Sciences Building, 567 Wilson Road, East Lansing, MI
48824, USA.
E-mail: lenski@msu.edu
Received 21 December 2016; revised 2 March 2017; accepted
10 March 2017; published online 16 May 2017
The ISME Journal (2017) 11, 2181–2194

www.nature.com/ismej

millions of cells that provide a continual supply of
new mutations. The populations are propagated in a
glucose-limited minimal salts medium at 37 °C by
transferring 1% of the volume into fresh medium
every day. The 100-fold dilution and resulting
regrowth allows log2 100≈6.7 generations each day.
Samples
from
each population
are
periodically
stored at −80 °C, where they are available for later
study. Importantly, the frozen cells remain viable,
such that changes in performance can be analyzed at
later times; and when accidents occur, the popula-
tions are restarted from the most recent whole-
population samples. As of this writing, the LTEE
has passed 66 000 generations.
Since
its
inception,
the
LTEE
has
examined
several overarching questions (Lenski et al., 1991).
Is the process of adaptation by natural selection
invariably slow and gradual, or are there periods of
rapid change and stasis? Does fitness eventually
reach
some
maximum
level,
or
can
organisms
continue to improve indefinitely, even in a constant
environment? Will the replicate populations achieve
the same fitness peaks, or will some discover better
solutions than others? If fitness trajectories evolve in
parallel, does that imply the same underlying genetic
changes? How are phenotypic and genetic evolution
coupled, both dynamically and functionally?
Dynamics of adaptation by natural selection
We can directly measure the extent of adaption by
natural selection by competing bacteria from a later-
generation
sample
against
the
ancestral
strain.
Relative fitness is expressed as the ratio of the
realized growth rates of the evolved and ancestral
bacteria as they compete with one another. Unless
otherwise stated, the competitions are performed in
the same medium and conditions as the LTEE;
however, we can also vary the conditions to examine
how that affects performance. The competitions
usually begin with an equal mix of ancestral and
evolved bacteria, but we sometimes vary the starting
ratio to look for more complex frequency-dependent
interactions. Of course, we must be able to distin-
guish the ancestral and evolved bacteria to enumer-
ate them and calculate their realized growth rates. To
that end, we use two variants of the ancestral strain
that differ by a genetic marker that allows us to
distinguish the competitors; the marker is neutral
(that is, does not affect fitness) under the conditions
of the LTEE. Before the ancestral and evolved
competitors are mixed, both have been frozen,
thawed and grown separately for a full transfer cycle
under the conditions where they will compete. This
acclimation ensures that any significant differences
in competitive fitness reflect genetic differences
rather
than
non-heritable
differences
in
physiological state.
Looking at the fitness trajectory for one population
over
the
first
2000
generations
(Lenski
and
Travisano, 1994), we see that fitness increased by
~ 30% (Figure 1a). The rise appears to involve three
discrete steps of ~ 10% each. This pattern closely
matches the dynamic one expects in a large, initially
homogeneous asexual population. Consider a muta-
tion that confers a 10% benefit. Assuming it is not
lost to random genetic drift while it is rare, then it
takes ~ 250 generations for that mutation to become
the majority. For most of that time the mutant
remains a tiny minority because, assuming a con-
stant growth-rate differential, the ratio of the mutant
to its progenitor changes exponentially. Therefore,
the fitness trajectory, at least in the early generations,
is dominated by sequential selective sweeps of a few
mutations with large beneficial effects. Other bene-
ficial mutations occur as well, but they are out-
competed
by
the
most
beneficial
ones,
a
phenomenon
called
clonal
interference
(Gerrish
and Lenski, 1998; Maddamsetti et al., 2015). When
clones from this population were sequenced, five
mutations were found and each mutation was shown
to be beneficial (Khan et al., 2011). The fact that
there were five beneficial mutations, despite only
three step-like increases in fitness, indicates that
some sweeps involved multiple beneficial mutations
(Lang et al., 2013; Maddamsetti et al., 2015).
Figure 1
Fitness trajectories of evolving E. coli populations. (a) Fitness trajectory for one population, Ara–1, relative to its ancestor over
the first 2000 generations of the LTEE. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals based on replicated assays. The line segments show the fit
of a step model to the data. Modified from Lenski and Travisano (1994). (b) Trajectory for the grand-mean fitness across the LTEE
populations over 50 000 generations. Error bars are 95% confidence limits based on replicate populations. The curve shows the fit of a
power-law model. Modified from Wiser et al. (2013).
Dynamics of adaptation and genome evolution
RE Lenski
2182
The ISME Journal

We have also characterized the grand-mean fitness
trajectory
across
the
replicate
populations
and
50 000 generations (Wiser et al., 2013). Over this
timeframe, the bacteria reached a relative fitness of
~ 1.7, meaning they grew ~ 70% faster than their
ancestor when competing in the LTEE environment
(Figure 1b). Their rate of improvement slows over
time, as it becomes more difficult to achieve further
gains after taking the low-hanging fruit. Does this
slowdown imply that the bacteria have, or eventually
will, hit some limit on their fitness? Wiser et al.
(2013) compared the fit of two simple models with
these data, each of which has two free parameters.
One model, a rectangular hyperbola, has an asymp-
tote. The other model, a power-law, has no upper
bound, but the rate of increase declines with the
logarithm of time. Both models fit the data well, but
the power-law model fits the data better. Moreover,
the power-law relation is much better at predicting
the future than the hyperbolic model. When a
truncated data set was used to predict the future
trajectory,
the
hyperbolic
model
systematically
underestimated the potential for further fitness gains.
By contrast, the power-law model predicted with
impressive accuracy the improvement out to 50 000
generations using only 5000 generations of data
(Wiser et al., 2013).
The power-law model has no upper bound, and so
one might reasonably worry that it predicts the
bacteria will eventually grow at a rate that is
biophysically implausible. However, it does not
predict implausible growth rates for the foreseeable
future because the rate of improvement scales with
the logarithm of time. The ancestral strain used to
found the populations had a doubling time of
~ 55 min in the glucose-limited minimal medium of
the LTEE (Vasi et al., 1994). Wiser et al. (2013)
extrapolated the model to 2.5 billion generations,
which corresponds to 50 000 generations of scien-
tists running the LTEE for 50 000 generations each.
At
that
point,
the
projected
doubling
time
is
~ 23 min.
That
value
would
be
impressive
for
bacteria growing in a minimal medium, but it is no
faster than many E. coli strains can grow in nutrient-
rich media, and some species can grow even faster.
Thus, the power-law model generates plausible
predictions far into the future.
One might also ask whether it is appropriate to
base inferences about the dynamics of adaptation on
competitions against an ancestor that is increasingly
distant in time. This approach implicitly assumes
that relative fitnesses are transitive; for example, if
strain B is 10% more fit than strain A, and strain C is
10% more fit than B, then we expect C to be 21%
more fit than A when relative fitnesses are multi-
plicative.
In
most
natural
circumstances,
this
assumption would be unreasonable over long peri-
ods, and it would not be met in many laboratory
systems
with
complex
ecological
feedbacks
mediated by predators, secreted metabolites and
the like. However, this assumption appears to be
valid in the LTEE, at least to a first approximation
and in most cases, based on assays involving
competitors from different generations (de Visser
and Lenski, 2002). The extreme simplicity of the
LTEE environment undoubtedly accounts for the
transitivity; in particular, the low concentration of
glucose limits the population density, which in turn
limits
the
accumulation
of
by-products
in
the
medium. Nonetheless, as discussed below, subtle
frequency-dependent
interactions
involving
by-
products have arisen in some populations, but they
have fitness effects that are small in comparison with
the overall gains in fitness relative to the ancestor. In
any case, to the extent that fitness trajectories based
on competition against the ancestor are inaccurate,
they should generally underestimate the extent of
continuing adaptation (Wiser et al., 2013). That is
because genotypes that systematically increase in
frequency in large populations must be more fit than
those they replace, but that need not be the case
relative to some type that is no longer present
(Paquin and Adams, 1983).
Evolving complexity
The LTEE was designed to be simple. Having just
one species, one limiting resource and no spatial
structure should minimize complex ecological inter-
actions, and the absence of horizontal gene transfer
was meant to simplify genetic analyses. Nonetheless,
unexpected and interesting complexities arose spon-
taneously as a consequence of the bacteria evolving
within these narrow confines.
On the ecological front, one population, called
Ara–2, has diverged into two distinct lineages, called
L and S, which have coexisted for over 50 000
generations.
There
are
at
least
two
ways
that
coexistence could occur, even in this simple envir-
onment. First, one ecotype might grow faster at the
concentration of glucose available at the start of each
day, whereas the other type may grow relatively
faster as the concentration is drawn down. Second,
one type might be the superior competitor for the
glucose, whereas the other better uses some secreted
by-product, generating a cross-feeding interaction. In
population Ara–2, coexistence depends primarily on
the second mechanism. The L ecotype grows faster
on glucose, but it cannot grow in its own spent
medium, which the S type is able to use (Rozen and
Lenski, 2000). It appears that acetate is the main by-
product that supports the S lineage (Großkopf et al.,
2016). During the establishment of this polymorph-
ism, the L ecotype lost its ability to use acetate
whereas the S type improved that ability. As a result
of the trade-off between growth on glucose and
acetate, the two ecotypes can stably coexist. That is,
each type has a competitive advantage when rare,
but as its frequency increases, it loses its advantage.
However, evolution has continued in both lineages
(Le Gac et al., 2012). As one or the other acquired
new
beneficial
mutations,
they
perturbed
the
Dynamics of adaptation and genome evolution
RE Lenski
2183
The ISME Journal

relationship, leading to large fluctuations in their
relative abundance over longer periods (Rozen and
Lenski, 2000). In principle, one ecotype might evolve
in such a way that it drives the other extinct, but that
has not yet happened in population Ara–2.
Other populations generated more transient poly-
morphisms (Maddamsetti et al., 2015). In population
Ara–1,
two
lineages
coexisted
from
~ 7000
to
~ 14 000 generations, before one drove the other
extinct (Figure 2). It is not known why the poly-
morphism in Ara–2 has persisted longer than those
in other populations, but a likely explanation is that
the L ecotype lost its ability to use acetate. In other
populations, the ecotype that is the better competitor
for glucose might retain its ability to use acetate. If
so, the advantage to a minority ecotype with better
growth on acetate would be less, and a smaller
improvement in the dominant type might be suffi-
cient to drive the minority type to extinction.
On
the
genetics
front,
complexity
arose
via
changes in the mutation rate (Sniegowski et al.,
1997; Barrick et al., 2009; Blount et al., 2012;
Tenaillon et al., 2016). Six populations evolved
hypermutability caused by mutations affecting either
DNA mismatch repair or the ability to remove certain
oxidized bases. The changes are not subtle, with
increases in the point mutation rate of ~ 100-fold,
although several populations later evolved reduced
hypermutability (Figure 3). The hypermutability
affects not only the mutation rate but also the
spectrum of base substitutions. In addition to the
populations that evolved higher point mutation
rates, population Ara+1 evolved increased activity
of a native transposable element, IS150, which led to
increased rates of insertion mutations as well as
chromosomal rearrangements (Papadopoulos et al.,
1999; Raeside et al., 2014; Tenaillon et al., 2016).
These
changes
complicate
genetic
analyses.
In particular, the increased mutation rates make it
more difficult to identify the ‘driver’ mutations that
improve fitness because they are surrounded by
many more ‘passenger’ mutations that are neutral or
even deleterious. (Nevertheless, by focusing on
populations that did not evolve hypermutability,
and other lineages before they became hypermuta-
ble, we can identify genetic targets of selection in the
LTEE. I will return to that topic in a later section).
The emergence of hypermutators raises the ques-
tions of how and why they evolve. At first glance,
they might seem to evolve because their higher
mutation rate speeds the process of adaptation by
natural selection. That explanation is correct, but
also incomplete. Beneficial mutations are only a
small fraction of all mutations, and a random
mutation is more likely to be deleterious than
beneficial. From that perspective, a bacterium with
an increased mutation rate has a disadvantage
because its progeny tend to be less fit. However,
natural selection depends not only on average fitness

period between ~ 7000 and ~ 14 000 generations, when two major clades—one shown in shades of green, and the other in yellows and reds

Changing mutation rate in population Ara–1. This
population maintained the low ancestral mutation rate for over

Dynamics of adaptation and genome evolution
RE Lenski
2184
The ISME Journal

effects, but also on the variance in fitness, and a
hypermutable lineage may prevail if it produces the
next big winner. In an asexual population, the allele
that causes hypermutability is inherited along with
any beneficial mutation that a hypermutator happens
to produce, generating indirect selection for hyper-
mutability (Tenaillon et al., 2001). But if an allele that
causes hypermutability is usually at a disadvantage,
how does it become common enough to generate the
rare winner? In fact, most mutations that cause
hypermutability
will
never
produce
a
winner;
instead, they will go extinct. However, given recur-
rent mutations in the genes that encode the proteins
that perform mismatch repair and remove mutagenic
compounds, occasionally such a mutant will get
lucky before it goes extinct and produce a beneficial
mutation that more than offsets its harmful effect,
allowing the hypermutator to increase in frequency.
The probability that this happens depends on the
opportunity for beneficial mutations. As a general
tendency,
the further a
population
is
from
its
optimum, the more scope there is for improvement
and the greater the opportunity for beneficial muta-
tions
(Moore
et
al.,
2000;
Wilke
et
al.,
2003;
Kryazhimskiy et al., 2014). Consequently, when a
population encounters a new environment—such as
at the start of the LTEE—there are many opportu-
nities for hypermutators to generate beneficial muta-
tions
and
become
established.
Then,
as
the
population becomes better adapted to those condi-
tions, the opportunity for further improvement is
reduced while the cost of deleterious mutations
continues unabated. As a result, a lower mutation
rate may evolve once the fitness gain that results from
reducing the load of deleterious mutations becomes
greater than the gains associated with beneficial
mutations
that
the
hypermutator
can
generate
(Figure 3). In short, the mutation rate is subject to
an evolutionary tension between opposing effects
(Wielgoss et al., 2013; Good and Desai, 2016).
Innovation and contingency
The LTEE populations live in a medium with
glucose as the limiting resource. Citrate is also
present as a chelating agent, but most E. coli cannot
transport citrate into the cell when oxygen is present.
The inability to grow aerobically on citrate is one of
the defining features of E. coli as a species. Some
strains can consume citrate under anoxic conditions,
although
doing
so
involves
co-metabolism
and
requires another source of carbon and energy. After
~ 31 000 generations, however, bacteria in popula-
tion Ara–3 gained the ability to consume citrate in
the oxygen-rich LTEE environment (Blount et al.,
2008). Moreover, these Cit+ cells can grow on citrate
as a sole carbon source. This population was not
hypermutable when this new trait arose, although it
later evolved hypermutability. None of the other
populations has evolved this ability even after
465 000 generations. Given the population size,
number of generations, and ancestral mutation rate,
every point mutation has been tested many times
over in each population. Why, then, was it so
difficult to evolve the Cit+ phenotype?
One possibility is that the transition from Cit– to
Cit+ required multiple mutations, so that the right
genetic background had to be in place, after which
(and only after which) another mutation would yield
the new function. A second possibility is that some
rare type of mutation was necessary to produce the
Cit+ phenotype. These hypotheses are not mutually
exclusive; in fact, both factors contributed to the
difficulty of this transition under the conditions of
the LTEE. To examine the effect of genetic back-
ground, Blount et al. (2008) performed ‘replay’
experiments in which they attempted to evolve the
Cit+ phenotype starting from the ancestor and Cit–
clones isolated at various times. In light of the
difficulty of generating Cit+ mutants, most replays
involved plating large numbers of cells on an agar-
based medium that contained citrate but no glucose,
incubating the plates for several weeks, and seeing
whether any Cit+ mutants emerged. Although Cit+
mutants were very rare, the replays showed that
genetic context mattered: neither the ancestor nor
any clone that had been isolated before generation
20 000 produced any Cit+ mutants, but 17 mutants
arose from later clones. Thus, the origin of this new
function was historically contingent; that is, the
propensity to evolve the Cit+ phenotype depended
on one or more previous changes.
Whole-genome
sequencing
was
performed
to
identify the mutations responsible for the new
function (Blount et al., 2012). The ‘actualizing’
mutation that first produced a Cit+ cell was found
to be a tandem duplication involving a gene, citT,
which encodes a protein used to transport citrate in
the absence of oxygen. The effect of the duplication
was that the second copy of the gene was adjacent to
a
new
upstream
regulatory
region,
which
was
downstream of the original copy. As a consequence
of this ‘promoter capture’ event, the citT gene was
expressed in the presence of oxygen as glucose ran
out, allowing the cells to switch to growing on
citrate. All of the Cit+ mutants from the replay
experiments also had rearrangement mutations that
involve the citT gene and appear to enable expres-
sion from alternative promoters. Evidently, no point
mutation can generate growth on citrate, even in an
otherwise suitable genetic background. Moreover,
the relevant rearrangements must happen at very low
rates under the specific conditions of the LTEE. The
duplicated region then underwent further amplifica-
tion in population Ara–3, which increased its growth
on citrate (Blount et al., 2012).
To
see
how
genetic
context
affected
citrate
metabolism, the relevant module—the citT gene
and its newly captured regulatory region—were
moved onto a high-copy plasmid, which was then
transformed into four clonal backgrounds (Blount
et al., 2012). Three of the transformed clones,

including the ancestral strain, could grow on citrate
in the presence of oxygen, albeit with long delays
between the depletion of glucose and the start of
growth on citrate and other difficulties (Figure 4a).
By contrast, the transformant of a Cit– clone that was
closely related to the Cit+ lineage in population
Ara–3 made a seamless transition from glucose to
citrate and reached a high density (Figure 4b). These
results
indicate
epistasis
between
the
citrate-
transport module and genetic background. More
recent studies have identified chromosomal muta-
tions that, along with that module, enable vigorous
growth on citrate (Quandt et al., 2014, 2015).
As interesting as this function is from a genetics
perspective, it is equally interesting from an ecolo-
gical standpoint. When the Cit+ type evolved, it did
not drive the Cit– bacteria extinct, nor did the Cit+
bacteria lose their ability to grow on glucose; instead,
the two types coexisted for over 10 000 generations
before the Cit– lineage went extinct (Turner et al.,
2015). Coexistence was possible, in part, because the
Cit+ bacteria had a longer lag before growth than the
Cit– bacteria when they were transferred into fresh
medium (Blount et al., 2008). The Cit+ cells grew on
citrate before entering stationary phase, so they
probably had to change their metabolic state to a
greater extent than did the Cit– cells in order to grow
on glucose. Also, the evolution of Cit+ bacteria led to
even more complex ecological interactions as a
consequence of the biochemical mechanism they
use to obtain citrate. The citT gene encodes an
antiporter protein that, while bringing a citrate
molecule into the cell, exports a succinate, fumarate
or
malate
molecule
to
the
medium.
Citrate
is
energetically more valuable than these compounds,
but E. coli can nonetheless use them for growth. In
fact,
both
the
Cit–
and
Cit+
lineages
evolved
improved growth on succinate (Turner, 2015). Thus,
the interactions in this flask ecosystem became
increasingly complex as a consequence of evolution,
with competition for not one, not two, but several
potential sources of carbon and energy.
Genome dynamics
How many mutations have occurred in the LTEE?
How have they accumulated over time? In answering
these questions, it is critically important to distin-
guish between the number of mutational events that
have
occurred
and
the
number
of
mutational
differences between an evolved genome and its
ancestor. What follows is a rough approximation
for the former in a nonhypermutable population
through 50 000 generations. The generations took
7500 days of 100-fold dilution and regrowth; each
regrowth produced ~ 3 × 108 cells; each cell’s genome
has ~ 5 × 106 bp; and the point mutation rate is ~ 10–10
per bp per cell replication. The resulting product is
over one billion for point mutations alone, and even
more with insertions, deletions and other types of
mutations. However, the vast majority of mutations
are lost by random genetic drift during the daily
dilutions; many others are eliminated by natural
selection because they have deleterious effects; even
most beneficial mutations are lost by drift or out-
competed by other genotypes with more beneficial
mutations (that is, clonal interference).
And how many mutations have accumulated in
the
evolving
genomes?
Tenaillon
et
al.
(2016)
sequenced 264 clonal genomes from the LTEE
(2 clones from 11 time points and 12 populations)
and compared them with the ancestral genome to
identify the mutations. In total, they found over
17 000 mutations, although most were in the six
populations that evolved hypermutability. Clones
sampled at generation 50 000 from populations that
were not hypermutable averaged ~ 75 mutations in
their genomes, in contrast to the billion-plus muta-
tion events that occurred in each population. Those
75 or so mutations also pale in comparison with the
differences between E. coli and Salmonella (Ochman
et al., 1999), or between two E. coli isolates from
nature (Dixit et al., 2015). However, it is not
surprising because the time scale of the LTEE, while
long for an experiment, is a drop in the bucket of
evolutionary time.

Not all the mutations that accumulated in the
LTEE genomes are beneficial—some might be neu-
tral or even slightly deleterious mutations that
‘hitchhiked’ with beneficial mutations, and others
new mutations that have hardly been tested by
selection.
However,
two
lines
of
evidence
led
Tenaillon et al. (2016) to conclude that the majority
of the point mutations in the evolved clones from
nonhypermutable lineages were, in fact, beneficial.
First, the trajectory of accumulated mutations over
time was better fit by a model with two parameters: a
linear term describing the expected accumulation of
neutral
mutations;
and
a
curvilinear
term
that
describes the declining rate at which beneficial
mutations arise and fix, as reflected in the declining
rate of fitness improvement. Although the fraction of
observed mutations that are beneficial falls as the
second
term
becomes
smaller
over
time,
most
mutations in the evolved genomes are beneficial
based on this analysis. The second line of evidence
compared the accumulation of nonsynonymous and
synonymous
mutations.
After
adjusting
for
the
number of sites at risk for each type, Tenaillon
et al. found an excess of nonsynonymous to synon-
ymous mutations in the evolved genomes of ~ 17-
fold over the first 500 generations of the LTEE and
~ 3.4-fold over 50 000 generations (Figure 5). The
same approach revealed an excess of point mutations
in intergenic regions of the evolved genomes.
Genetic targets of selection
The tandem duplication involving the citT gene was
clearly important in one population. More generally,
although, what genes have changed to improve
fitness by ~ 70%, on average, after 50 000 genera-
tions? The approaches used to find the genetic
targets of selection in the LTEE have changed over
the years, with observable phenotypic alterations
(Cooper et al., 2001, 2003) and changes in DNA
‘fingerprints’ (Papadopoulos et al., 1999; Schneider
et al., 2000; Woods et al., 2006) providing some ways
to track down and study mutations in years past.
Today, as reported above, whole-genome sequencing
allows one to find all of the mutations in a clone
(Velicer et al., 2006; Barrick et al., 2009; Deatherage
and Barrick, 2014), and whole-population metage-
nomic sequencing finds polymorphisms as well
(Barrick and Lenski, 2009; Lang et al., 2013). But
not all of the mutations thus found are beneficial;
some are mere hitchhikers. How can one separate the
wheat from the chaff to infer the genetic targets of
selection? One approach that has proven powerful in
the LTEE (Cooper et al., 2003; Woods et al., 2006), as
well as in other studies both experimental (Wichman
et al., 1999; Burke et al., 2010) and comparative
(Losos et al., 1998; Lieberman et al., 2011), is to look
for parallel evolution, that is, similar changes that
arose
repeatedly
in
independently
evolving
populations.
The hypermutability that evolved in some LTEE
lineages complicates the analysis of parallel evolu-
tion by increasing the numbers of other mutations
relative to the beneficial ones. Therefore, Tenaillon
et al. (2016) focused on samples from populations
that retained the ancestral mutation rate throughout
and others before they became hypermutable. They
found a strong signal of parallel evolution, with 57
genes that comprise only ~ 2% of the protein-coding
portion of the genome having half of the nonsynon-
ymous mutations in the evolved clones. Among the
genes that showed the strongest signals of parallel
changes are ones with core metabolic and regulatory
functions including pyruvate kinase, peptidoglycan
synthesis,
DNA
supercoiling
and
the
stringent
response. For several of these genes, isogenic strains
that differ by a single mutation have been con-
structed and tested in competition, and the muta-
tions
were
usually
confirmed
to
be
beneficial
(Cooper et al., 2003; Crozat et al., 2005; Pelosi
et al., 2006; Barrick et al., 2009). In most cases,
however, the reason that a mutation is beneficial is
not known. A plausible (but unproven) hypothesis is
that many of these mutations fine-tune the regulation
and expression of multiple functions to better match
cellular requirements in the simple, predictable
environment of the LTEE.
In addition to the parallel nonsynonymous sub-
stitutions, Tenaillon et al. (2016) also found numer-
ous parallel deletions of genes and blocks of linked
genes.
Many
of
these
genes
were
horizontally
acquired before the start of the LTEE (that is, present
in
the
ancestral
strain),
including
remnants
of
prophages and toxin–antitoxin modules typically
introduced by plasmids; some other deleted genes

encode host-specific functions including the produc-
tion of extracellular capsules and fimbriae. The
average
genome
size
declined
by
~ 1.4%
over
